105648.e: The hard core of the date is the seed itself and not a stone made from the fruit wall. That is why the date is a one-seeded berry.
105648.m: Even a fruit with only one seed can be a berry.

105649.q: Which vegetable is botanically also a berry?
105649.e: The pepper (capsicum) develops from an ovary and has a fleshy fruit wall with many seeds inside. Carrot, leek and kohlrabi, on the other hand, are root, leaves or shoot.
105649.m: The pepper is a vegetable, but botanically a berry.

105650.q: Which type of fruit is the cherry?
105650.e: The cherry has a thin skin on the outside, juicy flesh beneath it and a hard stone inside. These three layers are typical of stone fruits.
105650.m: A cherry is a stone fruit with a hard core.

105651.q: From which part does the hard stone of a stone fruit develop?
105651.e: The fruit wall of a stone fruit has three layers. The innermost layer becomes woody and forms the stone, which protects the seed.
105651.m: The stone is the woody inner layer of the fruit wall.

105652.q: What is inside the hard stone of a plum?
105652.e: The stone is only the protective shell. Inside it lies the actual seed, from which a new tree can grow.
105652.m: The seed lies inside the stone of a stone fruit.

105653.q: Which of these tropical fruits is a stone fruit?
105653.e: The mango has a large, flat stone in the middle that contains the seed. Around it lies the juicy, fibrous flesh.
105653.m: The mango is a stone fruit with a large, flat stone.

105654.q: Despite its name, the coconut is not a true nut. What is it botanically?
105654.e: The hard brown shell of the coconut is the woody inner fruit wall. That is why it counts as a stone fruit, just like the peach.
105654.m: The coconut is botanically a stone fruit.

105655.q: From which stone fruit is a well-known cooking oil pressed?
105655.e: The olive has oil-rich flesh and a hard stone. Sunflower, rape and flax form other types of fruit.
105655.m: Olive oil comes from a stone fruit.

105656.q: Which part of a stone fruit do we eat in the almond?
105656.e: The almond is a stone fruit with a leathery, not juicy, outer layer. We eat the seed that lies inside the stone.
105656.m: With the almond we eat the seed from inside the stone.

105657.q: Which plant family do cherry, plum and apricot belong to?
105657.e: These fruit trees belong to the genus Prunus within the rose family. Apple, pear and rose also belong to this large family.
105657.m: Many kinds of stone fruit belong to the rose family.

105658.q: In everyday language, what is fruit such as plums, peaches and apricots called as a group?
105658.e: Because these fruits have a hard stone, they are grouped together as stone fruit. Apples and pears, on the other hand, are called pome fruit.
105658.m: Fruit with a hard stone is called stone fruit.

105659.q: What is typical of a true nut?
a: The whole fruit wall becomes woody
105659.e: In a true nut the whole fruit wall becomes hard and woody. Inside there is usually only one single seed.
105659.m: In a true nut the whole fruit wall is hard.

105660.q: Which of these fruits is a true nut?
105660.e: The hazelnut has all the features of a true nut: the whole fruit wall is woody and it does not open. Many other so-called nuts are botanically something else.
105660.m: The hazelnut is a true nut.

105661.q: What are the three-sided nuts of the common beech called?
105661.e: The common beech forms small, three-sided nuts in a prickly husk. They are called beechnuts or beech mast.
105661.m: The fruits of the beech are called beechnuts.

105662.q: What do you call the bowl-shaped structure that an acorn sits in?
105662.e: The acorn is a nut whose bottom sits in a scaly cup. This cup grows out of the flower cluster.
105662.m: The acorn sits in a cup.

105663.q: A sunflower seed is really a whole small fruit. What is its striped shell?
105663.e: What we buy as a sunflower seed is a whole fruit. The striped shell is the fruit wall, and the seed lies inside.
105663.m: A sunflower seed is a small nut-like fruit.

105664.q: In a grain of wheat, the fruit wall and the seed have grown firmly together. So what is a grain of wheat really?
105664.e: A cereal grain is not just a seed but a whole fruit. Because the fruit wall and seed coat have grown together, they cannot be separated.
105664.m: A cereal grain is a whole fruit.

105665.q: Nuts are indehiscent fruits. What does that mean?
a: They do not open when ripe
They only grow in the shade
105665.e: Indehiscent fruits stay closed, and the seed is spread together with the fruit. Dehiscent fruits, on the other hand, open and scatter their seeds.
105665.m: An indehiscent fruit stays closed even when ripe.

105666.q: How many seeds does a true nut usually contain?
105666.e: A true nut usually has one seed. That is why you normally find only one kernel in a hazelnut.
105666.m: A true nut usually contains only one seed.

105667.q: What happens to a ripe capsule?
a: It grows together with the receptacle
105667.e: Capsules are dehiscent fruits. When ripe they dry out and open through slits, lids or holes.
105667.m: A ripe capsule opens and scatters its seeds.

105668.q: What does a capsule develop from?
105668.e: A capsule forms from at least two carpels that have grown together. That is why it often has several chambers.
105668.m: A capsule develops from several joined carpels.

105669.q: How do the seeds get out of a ripe poppy capsule?
a: Through small holes at the top when the wind shakes it
The capsule bursts with a bang
The capsule rots in the soil
105669.e: In the poppy, small holes open at the top under the disc of the stigma. When the stem sways in the wind, the seeds are scattered as if from a salt shaker. This is called a pore capsule.
105669.m: The poppy capsule scatters its seeds through small holes.

105670.q: Botanically, the prickly green case of the horse chestnut is a ...?
105670.e: The case of the horse chestnut splits into three parts when ripe. The shiny brown conkers inside are the seeds.
105670.m: The horse chestnut forms a prickly capsule with seeds inside.

105671.e: After flowering, the tulip grows an upright capsule with three chambers. Pea, cherry and hazelnut form other types of fruit.
105671.m: The tulip forms a capsule after flowering.

105672.q: In which crop are the valuable fibres long hairs on the seeds inside a capsule?
105672.e: The cotton capsule bursts open when ripe, and the white seed hairs puff out. Fabrics are made from these hairs.
105672.m: Cotton is made of seed hairs from a capsule.

105673.q: The so-called vanilla pod is not really a pod at all, botanically. What is it?
105673.e: The fruit of the vanilla orchid is a long capsule. In the shops it is still called a vanilla pod.
105673.m: The vanilla pod is really a capsule.

105674.q: Which plant do linseeds come from, which ripen in roundish capsules?
105674.e: Flax, also called linseed, forms small round capsules with shiny seeds. Linen fibres are also made from its stems.
105674.m: Linseeds are the seeds of flax.

105675.q: How does a ripe pod open?
105675.e: A pod develops from a single carpel. When ripe it splits open along the front seam and the back seam.
105675.m: A pod splits open along two seams.

105676.q: Where do the fruits of the peanut ripen?
105676.e: After fertilisation the flower stalk grows downwards and pushes the young ovary into the soil. The fruit ripens there.
105676.m: The peanut hides its pods in the soil.

105677.q: Which type of fruit is the peanut?
105677.e: The peanut is related to the pea and the bean. Its shell is a pod that usually contains two seeds.
105677.m: The peanut is not a nut but a legume.

105678.q: Which plant family do pea, bean and lentil belong to?
105678.e: Peas, beans, lentils and clover belong to the legumes. What they have in common is the pod.
105678.m: You can recognise legumes by their pods.

105679.q: Oilseed rape and mustard form long fruits with a dividing wall in the middle. What are they called?
105679.e: In the cabbage family, siliques develop from two carpels and have a thin dividing wall. Pods have no such wall.
105679.m: The cabbage family forms siliques, legumes form pods.

105680.q: From which legume is tofu made?
105680.e: To make tofu, soya beans are soaked, ground and cooked. The tofu is then set from the soya milk.
105680.m: Tofu is made from soya beans.

105681.q: Which bean with bright red flowers is also called the scarlet runner?
105681.e: The runner bean climbs high and stands out with its scarlet flowers. It forms long pods with large, often speckled seeds.
105681.m: The runner bean has red flowers and long pods.

105682.q: From which legume is hummus made?
105682.e: Hummus is a purée of cooked chickpeas with sesame paste. The chickpea forms short pods with one or two seeds.
105682.m: Hummus is made mainly of chickpeas.

105683.q: What is special about an aggregate fruit such as the raspberry?
a: Many little fruits from one flower form one fruit
It grows together from many trees
It has no pips at all
105683.e: In the raspberry flower many little fruits form side by side. Together they make a single fruit, the aggregate fruit.
105683.m: An aggregate fruit consists of many little fruits from one flower.

105684.q: Botanically, what is a single red bead of a raspberry?
105684.e: Each bead has a tiny hard stone inside. The raspberry is therefore an aggregate of stone fruits.
105684.m: The raspberry consists of many small stone fruits.

105685.q: When picking, how can you tell a raspberry from a blackberry?
105685.e: The raspberry comes away from the cone-shaped receptacle, which stays on the plant. With the blackberry the receptacle is picked too.
105685.m: A picked raspberry is hollow inside.

105686.q: What are the little yellow dots on the outside of a strawberry?
105686.e: Each dot is a tiny nut with a seed inside. The red flesh is only the enlarged receptacle.
105686.m: The real fruits of the strawberry are the little nuts on the outside.

105687.q: Which fruit, like the raspberry, is an aggregate of stone fruits?
105687.e: The blackberry also consists of many small stone fruits that come from a single flower. Bilberry, redcurrant and gooseberry, on the other hand, are true berries.
105687.m: Blackberry and raspberry are aggregates of stone fruits.

105688.q: What does a pineapple develop from?
a: From many flowers that grow together
105688.e: In the pineapple the fruits of many flowers in a whole flower cluster grow together into one single large fruit. This is called a multiple fruit.
105688.m: A pineapple develops from many flowers that have grown together.

105689.q: What colour are the flowers of the meadow buttercup in our fields?
105689.e: The buttercup flowers shiny yellow in spring and summer. After flowering it forms a small head of many little nuts.
105689.m: The buttercup has shiny yellow flowers.

105690.q: What do the split-open fruits of the peony contain in autumn?
105690.e: The fruits of the peony open along a seam. Inside lie shiny black or dark blue seeds.
105690.m: The peony forms fruits with shiny seeds.

a: A fruit that other flower parts help to form
A fruit that only ripens at night
105691.e: A true fruit develops only from the ovary. In a false fruit, other parts such as the receptacle also grow into the fruit.
105691.m: In a false fruit the receptacle also helps to build the fruit.

105692.q: Which part of the apple is the real fruit from the ovary?
105692.e: The juicy flesh of the apple grows from the receptacle. Only the papery core with the pips develops from the ovary.
105692.m: In the apple the core is the true fruit.

105693.q: Which fruit, like the apple, has a core with pips in the middle?
105693.e: Apple, pear and quince are pome fruits with a core. Cherry, plum and peach are stone fruits with a hard stone.
105693.m: Apple and pear are pome fruits.

105694.q: What does the red, juicy flesh of the strawberry develop from?
105694.e: After flowering the receptacle swells up a lot and becomes red and sweet. That is why the strawberry is also a false fruit.
105694.m: Strawberry flesh is an enlarged receptacle.

105695.q: What is the red fruit of the wild rose called?
105695.e: After flowering, the wild rose forms red fruits. They are called rose hips. People make tea and jam from them.
105695.m: The rose hip is the fruit of the rose.

105696.q: What is inside a rose hip?
105696.e: Inside the rose hip there are lots of hard little nuts with fine hairs. These hairs make your skin itch and used to be used as itching powder.
105696.m: Inside the rose hip lie many hairy little nuts.

105697.q: What is the juicy so-called cashew apple made of?
105697.e: On the cashew tree the stalk below the fruit thickens into a juicy ‘apple’. The real fruit is the kidney-shaped nut attached to it.
105697.m: The cashew apple is a thickened stalk and not a true fruit.

105698.q: What does the fig enclose with its fleshy tissue?
105698.e: The fig is a jug-shaped flower cluster with its flowers on the inside. From them come many tiny little fruits that crunch when you eat them.
105698.m: A fig is a flower cluster that has grown inwards.

105699.q: What are seeds that are spread by the wind like?
a: Light, often with wings or hairs
105699.e: Light seeds with wings or fine hairs are carried far by the wind. Examples are the maple and the dandelion.
105699.m: Wind-spread seeds are light and often have wings or hairs.

105700.q: How do dandelion fruits get far away?
a: They fly on a little parachute in the wind
105700.e: Each little dandelion fruit has a parachute of fine hairs. Like a parachute, it floats away on the wind.
105700.m: The dandelion flies with little parachutes.

105701.q: Which tree has winged fruits that spin to the ground like propellers?
105701.e: The fruit of the maple splits into two parts, each with a wing. As they fall they spin and stay in the air longer.
105701.m: Maple fruits spin like little propellers as they fall.

105702.q: What is the large, narrow bract on the fruit cluster of the lime tree for?
105702.e: The bract has grown together with the stalk of the fruits. It makes the whole fruit cluster glide through the air as it spins.
105702.m: Lime fruits glide away with a wing-like leaf.

105703.q: Which plants have especially tiny, dust-like seeds that the wind carries far?
105703.e: Orchid seeds are as small and light as dust. But they contain hardly any nutrients and need the help of fungi to germinate.

105704.q: In early summer, white fluff sometimes flies through the air. Which trees does it often come from?
105704.e: Poplars and willows form seeds with long white hairs. The wind carries them far away as fluffy flakes.
105704.m: The white fluff in early summer often comes from poplar seeds.

105705.q: What are plants called that dry out and are rolled whole by the wind across open land?
105705.e: In tumbleweeds the dry, ball-shaped plant breaks off at the root. As it rolls along it loses its seeds on the way.
105705.m: Tumbleweeds roll with the wind and scatter seeds.

105706.q: How does the poppy spread its seeds with the help of the wind?
a: The wind shakes the capsule like a shaker
105706.e: The poppy capsule sits on a long, springy stalk. When it sways in the wind, the seeds are thrown out bit by bit.
105706.m: The poppy is a wind shaker.

105707.q: Which of these seeds is typically spread by animals?
a: The burdock with its little hooks
105707.e: The burdock catches in the fur of animals with its little hooks and is carried far. Dandelion and maple use the wind, the coconut uses water.
105707.m: Burrs travel in the fur of animals.

105708.q: How do the fruits of the burdock get to new places?
a: They cling to animal fur with hooks
They are carried far by the wind
They are thrown out of the fruit
105708.e: Burrs have small hooks. With them they get caught in fur or feathers and fall off somewhere later. They were the model for Velcro.
105708.m: Burrs travel on the outside of animals’ fur.

105709.q: How do birds take the seeds of many berries to new places?
a: They are eaten and passed out in droppings
They are built into the nest
They are blown by the beating wings
105709.e: Birds eat the flesh, and the hard seeds pass through the gut undamaged. With the droppings they land in a new place, complete with fertiliser.
105709.m: Birds sow berry seeds with their droppings.

105710.q: Which bird hides lots of acorns in autumn and so helps oaks to spread?
105710.e: The jay buries acorns as a winter store. It does not find many of them again, and young oaks can grow from them.
105710.m: The jay’s forgotten stores grow into new oaks.

105711.q: Which animals carry off seeds with a nutritious attachment called an elaiosome?
105711.e: The elaiosome is an attachment on the seed that is rich in fat and protein. Ants carry the seed into their nest, eat the attachment and leave the seed.
105711.m: Ants spread seeds that have a treat attached.

105712.q: How do the seeds of mistletoe get onto other tree branches?
a: The wind carries them with wings
They jump out of the fruit
105712.e: Mistletoe berries contain a very sticky slime. Birds pass the seeds out or wipe them off on a branch, where they stick and germinate.
105712.m: Mistletoe gets birds to take its sticky seeds onto branches.

105713.q: Why are many ripe berries a striking red or black colour?
105713.e: Birds see colours well and recognise ripe berries by their colour. Unripe fruits are often green and inconspicuous.
105713.m: Bright berry colours are a signal for birds.

105714.q: Which mammal spreads hazelnuts and beechnuts by burying supplies in the ground?
105714.e: Squirrels make lots of hiding places in autumn. Whatever they do not find again in winter can germinate in spring.
105714.m: Squirrels plant new trees without meaning to.

105715.q: How are fruits that can float spread?
105715.e: Floating fruits are carried away by streams, rivers or ocean currents. Experts call this hydrochory, from the Greek word ‘hydor’ for water.
105715.m: Fruits that float are spread by water.

105716.q: Which fruit can drift in the sea for weeks and germinate on faraway coasts?
105716.e: The coconut has a thick, fibrous, air-filled husk. So it floats and can drift across the sea for months before germinating on a beach.
105716.m: Coconuts travel across the sea by floating.

105717.q: Which tree on the banks of streams has small fruits that can float?
105717.e: The little nuts of the black alder contain air-filled tissue and float on the water. In this way the alder settles new places along the bank.
105717.m: The alder sends its fruits floating down the stream.

105718.q: What helps many fruits and seeds to float on water?
105718.e: Air-filled spaces make a fruit lighter than water. A waxy surface also stops it from soaking up water.
105718.m: Air in the tissue makes seeds able to float.

105719.q: In mangroves the seeds already germinate on the parent plant. How are the seedlings spread?
a: They fall into the water and drift away
105719.e: The rod-shaped seedlings of mangroves come away from the tree and drift in the seawater. When they reach shallow mud, they quickly take root.
105719.m: Mangroves send ready-made seedlings on a journey.

105720.q: In which direction do streams and rivers mainly spread seeds?
105720.e: Flowing water carries everything down the valley with the current. That is why you often find riverbank plants along a whole river.
105720.m: Rivers carry seeds downstream with the current.

105721.q: What does a seed need to survive a long journey in seawater?
105721.e: Salt water would damage the seedling. A tight, hard shell protects the seed until it is washed ashore.
105721.m: A tight shell protects sea-going seeds from salt water.

105722.q: Some plants use the rain to spread their seeds. How does that work?
a: Raindrops splash the seeds out of the fruit
Raindrops stick the seeds to birds
Rain makes the seeds germinate at once
Rain dissolves the seeds in the soil
105722.e: In some plants the fruit works like a cup or a seesaw. When a raindrop hits it, the seeds splash out.
105722.m: Some plants use the force of raindrops.

105723.q: What does self-dispersal mean in plants?
a: The plant spreads its seeds without wind, water or animals
The plant keeps growing without seeds
The plant lets birds eat its seeds
The plant is sown by people
105723.e: Self-dispersing plants fling their seeds away or simply let them drop. They need no help from wind, water or animals.
105723.m: In self-dispersal the plant spreads its seeds itself.

105724.q: Which plant has the nickname ‘touch-me-not’ because its fruits burst open when touched?
105724.e: The ripe capsules of balsam are under tension. Even a light touch makes them roll up and fling the seeds away.
105724.m: Balsam flings its seeds away when touched.

105725.q: What causes the tension in the capsules of balsam?
a: warmth from the sun in the seed
105725.e: The cells of the fruit wall are tightly filled with water. This inner pressure builds up a tension that is suddenly released when the capsule is touched.
105725.m: Water pressure in the cells tightens the balsam capsule.

105726.q: Which plant squirts its seeds out of the fruit together with juice when ripe?
105726.e: In the squirting cucumber a high pressure builds up in the fruit. When it comes off the stalk, a jet of juice and seeds shoots out.
105726.m: The squirting cucumber shoots out its seeds in a jet of juice.

105727.q: How does broom fling its seeds away?
a: The drying halves of the pod twist
105727.e: As the pod walls dry out, they shrink unevenly. Suddenly the pod splits open, the halves twist and fling the seeds away.
105727.m: Broom pods burst open as they dry and fling out seeds.

105728.q: Which plant is named after the beak-like shape of its fruit and flings its seeds away?
105728.e: The fruit of the cranesbill looks like a long bird’s beak. When ripe, the parts roll up with a jerk and catapult the seeds.

105729.q: How do the heavy fruits of the horse chestnut reach the ground without outside help?
a: They fall because of their weight
They are carried far by the wind
They float away on the water
105729.e: Heavy fruits simply fall to the ground because of gravity. So they usually land under or near the parent plant.
105729.m: Heavy fruits fall to the ground because of their weight.

105730.q: What is usually the disadvantage of self-dispersal compared with wind dispersal?
a: The seeds land near the parent plant
105730.e: Flinging or falling usually takes seeds only a few metres. The young plants then compete with the parent plant for light and water.
105730.m: Self-dispersing plants usually stay near the parent plant.

105731.q: What does it mean when a seed is dormant?
a: It does not germinate for now, even though it is damp and warm
105731.e: While dormant, the seed waits until certain conditions are met, for example until a winter has passed. Only then does it germinate.
105731.m: A dormant seed waits before germinating.

105732.q: What is the advantage of seed dormancy for plants in Switzerland?
a: It stops them germinating just before winter
105732.e: If a seed germinated in a warm autumn, the young seedling could freeze in winter. Dormancy moves germination to the spring.
105732.m: Seed dormancy protects seedlings from winter.

105733.q: What do many seeds of native trees need before they germinate?
105733.e: Many seeds only germinate after a long cold period. Gardeners copy the winter by keeping the seeds damp in the fridge.
105733.m: Many seeds need cold before they germinate.

105734.q: Why do people lightly scratch some very hard seeds before sowing them?
a: So that water can get in
So that birds do not eat them
105734.e: Some seed coats are so hard that no water can get in. Scratching lets the seed take in water, swell and germinate.
105734.m: Hard seed coats can be scratched so that they germinate.

105736.q: In 2005 a young plant grew from a seed about 2000 years old from Israel. Which plant?
105736.e: The seed came from excavations at the fortress of Masada. The date palm that grew from it was nicknamed ‘Methuselah’.
105736.m: Some seeds can still germinate after hundreds of years.

105737.q: How is seed stored in the huge seed vault on Svalbard?
105737.e: In the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, seed samples from all over the world are kept in cold rooms far below zero degrees. Cold and dryness greatly slow down the ageing of the seeds.
105737.m: Cold keeps seeds able to germinate for a long time.

105738.q: What do you call the store of dormant seeds that can still germinate, lying in the soil?
105738.e: There are often thousands of seeds in the soil that rest for years. When the soil is dug up, some suddenly germinate, for example poppies on freshly dug earth.
105738.m: A seed bank in the soil waits for its chance.

105739.e: A large, very hard capsule grows on the Brazil nut tree. Inside, many seeds lie tightly packed, and these are sold as Brazil nuts.
105739.m: Brazil nuts are seeds and not true nuts.

105740.q: In what weather do spruce cones open and release their winged seeds?
105740.e: When the cone scales dry out, they spread apart. The winged seeds fly especially well in dry air; when it is wet the cone closes again.
105740.m: Spruce cones open when it is dry.

105832.q: What is the tube-shaped pocket in the skin that a hair sits in called?
105832.e: The hair follicle wraps around the hair root like a small tube. In it, the hair is made and anchored.
105832.m: Every hair sits in a hair follicle.

105833.q: Which small muscle on the hair follicle makes the hair stand up when you are cold?
105833.e: A tiny muscle is attached to the hair follicle. When it contracts, the hair stands up and you get goose bumps.
105833.m: The hair erector muscle makes hairs stand up in the cold.

105834.q: Which cells in the hair follicle make sure a new hair can grow after one falls out?
105834.e: There are stem cells in the upper part of the hair follicle. They can divide again and again and build a new hair root.
105834.m: Stem cells in the hair follicle make new hair growth possible.

105835.q: What are the thick hairs on a cat’s muzzle called, whose follicles are surrounded by especially many nerves?
105835.e: Whiskers, also called vibrissae, are touch hairs. Their follicles have lots of nerves, so the cat can feel the slightest air movements and obstacles in the dark.

105836.q: What are the fine, short, pale little hairs called that grow on the cheeks and arms, for example?
105836.e: Vellus hairs are thin, short and hardly coloured, and they cover large parts of the skin. Hair on the head and eyebrows, by contrast, is thicker and strongly coloured.
105836.m: The fine fuzz on the skin is made of thin, pale little hairs.

105837.q: Do unborn babies in the womb already have hair?
a: Yes, a fine fuzz that usually falls out before birth
No, hair only grows after birth
Yes, thick hair on the head that never falls out
105837.e: Even an unborn baby grows a very fine fuzz all over its body. It is called lanugo and usually falls out before birth.
105837.m: Unborn babies have a fine fuzz of hair.

105838.q: Why can you feel even a very light touch on a single hair?
a: There are nerve endings around the hair follicle
The tip of the hair is a sense organ
The hair conducts electricity to the brain
105838.e: A fine network of nerve endings lies around every hair follicle. When the hair moves, the movement is detected at the root and reported to the brain.
105838.m: Hairs work like little feelers because their follicles are surrounded by nerves.

105839.q: What is an inflammation of the hair follicle, usually caused by bacteria, called?
105839.e: In folliculitis, hair follicles become inflamed, often because of bacteria. Small red bumps or tiny spots of pus appear around a hair.
105839.m: Folliculitis is an inflammation of hair follicles.

105840.q: Which property of keratin means hair does not dissolve when you wash it?
a: It does not dissolve in water
105840.e: Keratin is a fibrous protein that does not dissolve in water. It can soak up a little water and swell, but it stays stable.
105840.m: Keratin does not dissolve in water.

105841.q: Which group of substances does keratin belong to?
105841.e: Keratin is a protein made of long chains of amino acids. These chains are twisted into very strong fibres.
105841.m: Keratin is an especially strong protein.

105842.q: Which parts of animals are also mainly made of keratin?
a: The shells of beetles and crabs
105842.e: Hooves, claws, feathers, reptile scales and the outer covering of horns are made of keratin. Snail shells are made of lime, beetle shells of chitin.
105842.m: Hooves, claws and feathers are made of keratin, like our hair.

105843.q: Which chemical element in keratin is responsible for burnt hair smelling so unpleasant?
105843.e: Keratin contains many building blocks with sulphur. When it burns, sulphur compounds form that smell strong and unpleasant.
105843.m: The sulphur in keratin makes burnt hair stink.

105844.q: Which bonds in keratin are broken during a perm and joined again in a new shape?
105844.e: Sulphur bridges hold the keratin chains in their shape. A perm breaks them chemically, the hair is wound round curlers and the bridges are joined again in the new shape.
105844.m: A perm changes the sulphur bridges in keratin.

105845.q: Which cells of the epidermis make keratin?
105845.e: Keratinocytes are the most common cells in the epidermis. They make keratin and slowly move up to the surface as they do so.
105845.m: Keratinocytes are the cells that make keratin.

105846.q: Which layer of the skin is made of dead cells full of keratin?
105846.e: The horny layer is the outermost layer of the epidermis. Its dead, keratin-rich cells protect the body against water loss and germs.
105846.m: The horny layer protects the skin with dead keratin cells.

105847.q: What is the process called in which cells fill up with keratin and die?
105847.e: In keratinisation, cells fill with keratin, lose their nucleus and die. This is how hair, nails and the horny layer of the skin are formed.
105847.m: In keratinisation, living cells turn into firm horn.

a: The scales of the outermost layer of hair lie flat
105848.e: The outermost layer of a hair is made of keratin scales like roof tiles. When they lie flat, the hair reflects the light and shines.
105848.m: Flat hair scales make hair shine.

105849.q: What is the thickened lower end of the hair root called?
105849.e: The hair bulb is the onion-shaped swelling at the end of the hair root. There, the cells that the hair grows from divide.
105849.m: The hair bulb is at the lower end of the hair root.

105850.q: What does the hair papilla bring to the growing cells of the hair root?
105850.e: The hair papilla reaches up into the hair bulb from below and contains tiny blood vessels. Through it, the hair root gets oxygen and nutrients.
105850.m: The hair papilla supplies the hair root with blood.

105851.q: Which part of a hair is made of living cells?
105851.e: Living cells only divide in the hair root. As soon as they are pushed upwards, they harden and die, which is why having your hair cut does not hurt.
105851.m: Only the root of a hair is alive.

105852.q: What is the part of the hair that sticks out of the skin and can be seen called?
105852.e: The hair shaft is the visible hair above the skin. The hair root, on the other hand, is hidden in the hair follicle.
105852.m: The visible part of a hair is called the hair shaft.

105853.q: Where are the pigments made that give hair its colour?
a: In pigment cells in the hair root
105853.e: Pigment cells called melanocytes sit in the hair bulb. They pass the pigment on to the new hair cells as they form.
105853.m: Hair colour is made down in the hair root.

105854.q: Why can the police get DNA more easily from a hair pulled out with its root than from a cut hair?
a: The root contains cells with a nucleus
The root is longer than the shaft
105854.e: Cells with a nucleus, which holds the genetic information, are attached to the hair root. In the hardened hair shaft, hardly any of this is left.
105854.m: For a DNA trace, the hair root is more valuable than the shaft.

105855.q: What usually happens if you pull out a hair but the hair follicle stays undamaged?
a: A hair never grows there again
105855.e: As long as the hair follicle is intact, it makes a new hair. Only when the follicle is destroyed does nothing grow there any more.
105855.m: A pulled-out hair grows back from a healthy follicle.

105856.q: Where do cells divide so that a hair gets longer?
a: At the tip of the hair
In the middle of the hair shaft
On the scalp next to the hair
105856.e: Down in the hair root, cells divide very quickly and push the hair upwards. That is why a hair grows from the bottom and not at the tip.
105856.m: A hair grows from the root.

105857.q: Roughly how many hairs from the head does a healthy person lose each day?
105857.e: Losing about 50 to 100 hairs a day is normal. Most of these hairs are replaced by new ones growing back.
105857.m: Losing up to about 100 hairs a day is normal.

105858.q: In alopecia areata (patchy hair loss), what attacks the hair roots?
105858.e: In alopecia areata, the immune system wrongly turns against the hair roots. Round bald patches appear, which often grow back.
105858.m: In patchy hair loss, the body’s defences attack the hair roots.

105859.q: Which deficiency is a common cause of increased hair loss?
105859.e: Hair roots need a lot of iron because their cells divide quickly. That is why more hair often falls out when there is not enough iron.
105859.m: Iron deficiency can lead to hair loss.

105860.q: Why does hair fall out during many cancer treatments with chemotherapy?
a: The medicines damage cells that divide quickly
105860.e: Chemotherapy targets cells that divide quickly, like cancer cells. The cells of the hair roots also divide quickly and are affected; after treatment, the hair usually grows back.
105860.m: Chemotherapy also affects the fast-growing cells of the hair roots.

105861.q: After a high fever or severe stress, hair often falls out with a delay. After about how long?
105861.e: The strain sends many hairs into the resting phase at the same time. This lasts a few months, so the hair only falls out about 2 to 3 months later.
105861.m: Hair loss after a fever or stress often only shows months later.

105862.q: What happens to a hair before it falls out?
a: It stops growing and only sits loosely
It suddenly becomes twice as thick
105862.e: Every hair has a growth phase and then a resting phase. In the resting phase it no longer grows and finally falls out. A new hair pushes up behind it.
105862.m: A hair falls out at the end of its resting phase.

105863.q: Which organ can cause hair loss if it is overactive or underactive?
105863.e: The hormones of the thyroid gland control metabolism, including in the hair roots. If it works too hard or too little, the hair can thin.
105863.m: Thyroid problems can make hair fall out.

105864.q: What should you do if you lose an unusual amount of hair over a long time?
a: Have a doctor find out the cause
105864.e: Heavy or long-lasting hair loss can have many causes, such as deficiencies or illnesses. A doctor can find them with tests.
105864.m: If you notice unusual hair loss, a medical check-up helps.

105865.q: What are the bald areas at the temples called, which often appear first when someone starts going bald?
105865.e: In inherited hair loss, the hairline often moves back at the temples first. This is called a receding hairline.
105865.m: A receding hairline means the hair moves back at the temples.

105866.q: What is a bald spot on the top of the back of the head called, which recalls a hairstyle monks used to wear?
105866.e: Monks used to have a round patch on the back of the head shaved bald, called the tonsure. The bald patch that forms on top of the head in many men looks similar.
105866.m: The tonsure is a bald patch on the top of the head.

105867.q: What mainly decides whether a man goes bald?
105867.e: The most common baldness comes from inherited hair loss: from birth, the hair roots are sensitive to certain hormones made by the body. Hats or washing play no part in it.

105868.q: Why is the skin of a bald head especially at risk in summer?
a: It has no sun protection from hair
It is thicker than other skin
It has a poorer blood supply
105868.e: Hair shades the scalp. Without it, UV rays hit the skin directly, which is why a hat or sun cream is important.
105868.m: A bald head needs a hat or sun cream in summer.

105869.q: What is usually moved in a hair transplant?
a: The person’s own hair roots from the back of the head
105869.e: In a hair transplant, the person’s own hair follicles are taken from the back of the head and put into bald areas. There they keep growing.
105869.m: In a hair transplant, your own hair moves to a new place.

105870.q: Why does a ring of hair often remain at the back and sides of many bald heads?
a: The hair roots there are less sensitive by inheritance
You lie on it at night
105870.e: The hair roots at the back and sides of the head do not react to the hormones involved in inherited hair loss. That is why a ring of hair often remains there.
105870.m: The ring of hair stays because its roots are tougher.

105871.q: Roughly what share of men have visible inherited hair loss by the age of 50?
105871.e: Inherited hair loss is very common. By about 50, around half of all men are affected to a greater or lesser degree.
105871.m: About one man in two has hair loss by 50.

105872.q: Where does the hair usually get thinner when women have inherited hair loss?
a: At the parting on top of the head
Only at the nape of the neck
105872.e: In women, the hair usually thins over a wide area around the parting. Going completely bald is rare for them.
105872.m: In women, the hair usually gets thinner at the parting.

105873.q: Why does hair turn grey with age?
a: The hair roots make less pigment
105873.e: In the hair roots, pigment cells make the pigment melanin. With age these cells work less, and colourless hairs grow.
105873.m: Grey hair appears when the hair roots make less pigment.

105874.q: Do more grey hairs grow back if you pull out a grey hair?
a: No, only one hair grows from each follicle
Yes, two or three grow back
Yes, all the neighbouring hairs turn grey
105874.e: A hair follicle only ever makes one hair, and pulling one out does not affect the neighbouring follicles. Getting more grey hair comes only from getting older.
105874.m: Pulling out grey hairs does not make more grey hairs grow.

105875.q: Why does a hair without pigment look white?
a: Tiny air bubbles scatter the light
105875.e: Colourless hair contains tiny pockets of air. They scatter the light in all directions, a bit like snow, which is why the hair looks white.
105875.m: Air in the hair makes colourless hairs look white.

105876.q: Can a dark hair that has already grown turn grey overnight?
a: No, only hair that grows back is colourless
105876.e: The hair shaft is dead, and its pigment stays. A hair only turns grey if it grows out of the root already colourless.
105876.m: A hair that has grown does not lose its colour overnight.

105877.q: If you look closely, what is “grey” hair usually?
a: A mixture of coloured and white hairs
Hair with grey dust on it
105877.e: A single hair is usually either still coloured or already white. Only the mixture of both looks grey from a distance.
105877.m: Hair looks grey because of the mix of coloured and white hairs.

105878.q: From what age do many people get their first grey hairs?
105878.e: Many people get their first grey hairs between about 30 and 40. Exactly when depends strongly on their genes.
105878.m: The first grey hairs often appear between 30 and 40.

105879.q: Why do grey roots show again a few weeks after grey hair has been dyed?
a: The hair growing back is still colourless
The dye moves into the scalp
The dye is destroyed by light
The hair rejects the dye straight away
105879.e: Hair dye only works on hair that has already grown. Colourless hair keeps growing out of the root, and it can be seen at the scalp as roots.
105879.m: Dyed hair grows back in its natural colour at the root.

105880.q: What is the pigment called that gives hair and skin their colour?
105880.e: Melanin is made in special cells of the skin and hair roots. Depending on its type and amount, hair is blond, brown, black or red.

105881.q: Roughly what share of the hairs on the head are in the growth phase at the same time?
105881.e: Every hair has its own rhythm. The vast majority are growing, and only a small number are resting or about to fall out, which is why all your hair never falls out at once.
105881.m: Most hairs on the head are growing at the same time, only a few are resting.

105883.q: Roughly how long does the growth phase of a hair on the head last?
105883.e: A hair on the head usually grows for between 2 and 6 years without a break. Then it moves into the transition and resting phases.
105883.m: A hair on the head grows for several years.

105884.q: A hair grows 1 cm per month. How long is it after 3 years of non-stop growth?
105884.e: 3 years are 3 times 12, so 36 months. At 1 cm per month, the hair grows 36 times 1 cm, so 36 cm.
105884.m: To work out hair length, multiply the growth per month by the number of months.

105885.q: Why do eyelashes and eyebrows stay much shorter than the hair on your head?
a: Their growth phase is much shorter
They are not made of keratin
105885.e: Eyelashes and eyebrows only grow for a few months, then they fall out and are replaced. Hair on the head, by contrast, keeps growing for years.
105885.m: The short growth phase keeps eyelashes and eyebrows short.

105886.q: Lena’s hair is 20 cm long and grows 1.2 cm per month. How long is it after 10 months without a haircut?
105886.e: In 10 months the hair grows 10 times 1.2 cm, so 12 cm. 20 cm plus 12 cm makes 32 cm.
105886.m: Add the growth of all the months to the starting length.

105887.q: A person has 100,000 hairs on their head, and each grows 0.3 mm per day. How many metres of hair grow altogether per day?
105887.e: 100,000 times 0.3 mm makes 30,000 mm. Since 1000 mm make one metre, that is 30 m.
105887.m: Lots of small lengths add up to a long distance.

105888.q: A hair stops growing and rests for a while. What usually happens next?
a: It falls out and a new hair grows
It keeps growing twice as fast
It turns into a sweat gland
It stays on the head for ever
105888.e: Every hair goes through growth, a short transition and a resting time. Then it falls out, and a new hair grows from the same hair follicle.
105888.m: After its resting time, a hair falls out and is replaced.

105889.q: What is the skin under the nail called, on which the nail plate rests?
105889.e: The nail plate lies firmly on the nail bed and slowly slides forwards over it as it grows.
105889.m: The nail lies on the nail bed.

105890.q: Why does a healthy fingernail look pink?
a: Blood vessels in the nail bed show through
The nail plate is coloured pink
Light is bent red in the nail
105890.e: The nail plate is almost see-through. Below it lies the nail bed, which has a good blood supply, and its colour shows through.
105890.m: The pink of nails comes from the blood in the nail bed.

105891.q: In which area is the nail plate made?
a: In the nail matrix at the base of the nail
At the tip of the nail
At the side edge of the nail
105891.e: The nail matrix lies under the skin at the base of the nail. Its cells harden and push the nail plate forwards.
105891.m: The nail grows from the nail matrix at the base of the nail.

105892.q: What colour do nails often turn when the blood carries too little oxygen, for example in severe cold?
105892.e: Blood low in oxygen is darker. The nail bed then looks bluish through the see-through nail plate.
105892.m: Bluish nails show there is little oxygen in the blood.

105893.q: What job does the cuticle at the base of the nail have?
a: It protects the nail matrix from germs
It makes the nail grow faster
105893.e: The cuticle seals the gap between the skin and the nail. This means fewer germs reach the sensitive nail matrix.
105893.m: The cuticle seals the base of the nail against germs.

105894.q: How do toenails grow compared with fingernails?
105894.e: Toenails only grow about half as fast as fingernails. That is why a whole toenail takes around one to one and a half years to grow back.
105894.m: Toenails grow more slowly than fingernails.

105895.q: Roughly how long does it take for a whole fingernail to grow back?
105895.e: The nail slowly grows forwards from the nail matrix to the tip. It takes about half a year until it is completely renewed.
105895.m: A fingernail renews itself in about half a year.

105896.q: What forms when you trap your finger hard and blood flows under the nail?
a: A dark bruise under the nail
105896.e: The blow tears tiny vessels in the nail bed. The blood collects under the nail plate and shows through dark red to black.
105896.m: Trapping your finger can cause a bruise under the nail.

105897.q: What makes an ingrown toenail more likely?
a: Cutting the nail round instead of straight
105897.e: If the corners are cut round, the nail can grow sideways into the skin and make it inflamed. That is why toenails are cut straight.
105897.m: Cut toenails straight so they do not grow in.

105898.q: Which germs usually cause nail fungus?
105898.e: Nail fungus is usually caused by thread fungi that feed on keratin. Less often, yeasts or moulds are involved.
105898.m: Nail fungus is usually caused by thread fungi.

105899.q: Where do people especially often catch nail or foot fungus?
a: Barefoot at indoor pools, saunas and showers
105899.e: Fungal spores survive well on damp floors. If you walk barefoot there, you can easily pick them up; pool sliders protect you.
105899.m: Pool sliders protect against fungi at pools and in showers.

105900.q: What kind of surroundings do nail fungi especially like?
105900.e: Fungi grow best in damp warmth, for example in tight, sweaty shoes. Airy shoes and dry feet make life hard for them.

105901.q: How can you often recognise nail fungus?
a: The nail becomes yellowish, thick and brittle
The nail becomes shiny and pink
The nail grows twice as fast
The nail becomes see-through and soft
105901.e: With nail fungus, the nail usually turns whitish to yellowish brown. It becomes thicker and crumbly and can come away from the nail bed.
105901.m: A yellow, thick and brittle nail can be a sign of nail fungus.

105902.q: Why does treating nail fungus often take many months?
a: The healthy nail has to grow back slowly
The medicines only work after years
The fungus hides in the bone
105902.e: The infected nail does not become healthy again; it has to be replaced by healthy nail growing back. Because nails grow slowly, this takes time.
105902.m: Nail fungus is only cured when a healthy nail has grown back.

105903.q: Which skin condition often comes before nail fungus on the toes?
105903.e: Athlete’s foot between the toes is very common. If it is not treated, the fungi can spread to the toenails.
105903.m: Untreated athlete’s foot can spread to the nails.

105904.q: How can you catch nail fungus from other people?
a: By shaking hands on the phone
105904.e: Fungal spores cling to towels, socks and shoes. That is why you should not share these things with others.
105904.m: Your own towels and shoes protect you from nail fungus.

105905.q: Are fingernails or toenails more often affected by nail fungus?
105905.e: Toenails often spend a long time in warm, damp shoes and grow slowly. That is why they are infected much more often than fingernails.
105905.m: Nail fungus mainly affects the toenails.

105906.q: What helps in everyday life to prevent nail fungus?
a: Drying your feet and the gaps between your toes well
Letting your nails grow as long as possible
105906.e: Dry skin between the toes gives fungi little to hold on to. Fresh socks every day and airy shoes also help.

105907.q: What can trigger a new flare-up of psoriasis?
105907.e: Psoriasis often comes in flare-ups. Infections, stress or certain medicines can trigger a new flare-up.
105907.m: Stress and infections can make psoriasis worse.

a: Yes, through shared plates and cups
105908.e: Psoriasis develops within the body itself, triggered by the immune system and an inherited tendency. You cannot catch it from people who have it.

105909.q: On which parts of the body does psoriasis appear especially often?
a: Earlobes and tips of the toes
105909.e: Typical patches appear on the outer sides of the elbows and knees and on the scalp. But other areas can be affected too.
105909.m: Psoriasis often appears on the elbows, knees and scalp.

105910.q: What happens differently in the skin with psoriasis?
a: The epidermis renews itself far too quickly
The skin makes no more cells
The skin loses all its hair
The skin is broken down by fungi
105910.e: Normally the epidermis renews itself in around four weeks. With psoriasis this happens in a few days, so the cells pile up and form scales.
105910.m: With psoriasis, the epidermis grows back far too quickly.

105911.q: What do typical patches of psoriasis look like?
105911.e: The patches have sharp edges, are red and slightly raised. On top lie shiny, silvery scales.
105911.m: Silvery scales on red skin are typical of psoriasis.

105912.q: How do the fingernails often change with psoriasis?
a: They all fall off at once
105912.e: Many people with it have pitted nails with small dents in the nail plate. Yellowish-brown patches, known as oil spots, also occur.
105912.m: Pits in the nails can be a sign of psoriasis.

105913.q: Which additional problem can some people with psoriasis have?
105913.e: In some people with psoriasis, the joints also become inflamed. This is called psoriatic arthritis.
105913.m: Psoriasis can also inflame the joints.

105914.q: Which treatment for psoriasis uses light in a targeted way?
105914.e: In light therapy, the skin is exposed to UV light in a controlled way. This slows down the excessive inflammation and the rapid cell division.
105914.m: Controlled UV light can ease psoriasis.

105915.q: What part does the immune system play in psoriasis?
a: It wrongly triggers inflammation in the skin
People with psoriasis have none at all
It only attacks fungi in the skin
It has nothing to do with it
105915.e: In psoriasis, the body’s defences overreact and cause inflammation in the skin. Flare-ups can be triggered by infections or stress, for example.
105915.m: Psoriasis is an inflammation that comes from the immune system.

a: A spot where the hair grows in a spiral
A bald spot on the head
105916.e: At a hair whorl, the hair follicles are angled so that the hairs grow in a circle around a central point.
105916.m: At a hair whorl, the hair grows in a circle.

105917.q: Where do most people have their hair whorl?
a: On the top of the head towards the back
In the middle of the forehead
At the nape of the neck
105917.e: The typical hair whorl is on the top of the back of the head. From there the hair spreads out in all directions.
105917.m: The hair whorl is usually on the top of the back of the head.

105918.q: In which direction does the hair whorl turn in most people?
105918.e: Studies show that in most people the whorl on the back of the head turns clockwise. In a minority it turns anticlockwise.

105919.q: What is it called when someone has two hair whorls on their head?
105919.e: Some people have two whorls next to each other on the back of the head. This is called a double crown; the hair there is often hard to style.
105919.m: Two hair whorls are called a double crown.

105920.q: Why is it hard to comb hair at a whorl in a different direction?
a: The direction of growth is fixed by the hair follicles
The hair there is electrically charged
105920.e: The hair follicles sit at an angle in the skin and set the direction of growth. Combing cannot change this for good.
105920.m: The angled follicles decide which way the hair grows.

105921.q: For which animal are hair whorls traditionally recorded in its passport for identification?
105921.e: In a horse passport, the position of the hair whorls is drawn in as well as the markings. They are different on every horse and do not change.
105921.m: Horses can also be recognised by their hair whorls.

105922.q: When is it decided where a person’s hair whorl will be?
105922.e: The hair follicles and their direction already form in the unborn child. That is why the hair whorl stays in the same place for life.
105922.m: The hair whorl forms before birth.

105923.q: How are head lice usually passed on?
a: By jumping from head to head
Through water in the swimming pool
105923.e: Head lice can neither jump nor fly. They mainly crawl onto another head when hair touches directly.
105923.m: Head lice move from head to head when hair touches.

105924.q: People with which natural hair colour usually have the most hairs on their head?
105924.e: Blond hairs are especially thin, but usually more of them grow, often around 150,000. Redheads have thicker hairs, but fewer of them.
105924.m: Blond people usually have the most but thinnest hairs on their head.

a: A shampoo with an anti-fungal ingredient
105925.e: Special anti-dandruff shampoos contain ingredients against the yeast fungus on the scalp. This calms the skin, and it makes fewer flakes.
105925.m: Anti-dandruff shampoos work against the fungus on the scalp.

105926.q: Which kind of living thing often encourages greasy dandruff?
105926.e: A yeast fungus that feeds on sebum lives on the scalp. If it multiplies a lot, it irritates the skin and more flakes form.
105926.m: A yeast fungus on the scalp can encourage dandruff.

105927.q: What is the line called where the scalp on the forehead meets skin without hair?
105927.e: The hairline is the line where the hair on the head begins. When hair loss starts, it can move backwards.
105927.m: Where the hair begins on the forehead is the hairline.

105928.q: What do head lice feed on?
105928.e: Head lice bite into the scalp several times a day and suck blood. Their saliva causes the typical itching.
105928.m: Head lice suck blood from the scalp.

105929.q: Why does a small cut on the scalp often bleed a lot?
a: The scalp has an especially good blood supply
The blood in the head is thinner
Blood does not clot on the head
105929.e: The scalp is supplied by many blood vessels that feed the hair roots. That is why even a small wound there bleeds heavily.
105929.m: The scalp has a rich blood supply and bleeds heavily when injured.

105930.q: What is the yellowish, scaly crust called that many babies have on their scalp in the first months of life?
105930.e: Cradle cap is a harmless, greasy flaking of the scalp in babies. It usually disappears by itself after a few months.
105930.m: Cradle cap is a harmless scaly crust in babies.

105931.q: A load is pulled up 3 m with a fixed pulley. How much rope do you have to pull?
105931.e: With a fixed pulley the load moves exactly as far as the end of the rope you pull. For a lift of 3 m you pull 3 m of rope.
105931.m: With a fixed pulley, rope distance and lifting height are equal.

105932.q: Why is it more comfortable to pull up a load with a fixed pulley, even though it saves no force?
a: You can pull downwards and use your own weight
105932.e: The fixed pulley changes the direction of pull. If you pull downwards, you can use your body weight and stand more securely.
105932.m: A fixed pulley turns the force into a more comfortable direction.

105933.q: What is the axle of a fixed pulley attached to?
a: A fixed mounting, for example a beam
The free end of the rope
105933.e: The axle of a fixed pulley hangs in one place. The pulley only turns but does not move with the load.
105933.m: A fixed pulley turns on the spot.

105934.q: A person with a weight of 600 N hangs on the rope of a fixed pulley. What load can they just hold in balance, ignoring friction?
105934.e: On a fixed pulley the pulling force equals the load. With their whole weight of 600 N, the person can hold at most 600 N.
105934.m: On a fixed pulley you can hold at most as much as you weigh.

105935.q: What kind of lever can a fixed pulley be seen as?
a: A two-sided lever with equal arms
A one-sided lever with unequal arms
A two-sided lever with unequal arms
105935.e: The pivot is the axle, and the load and pull act left and right at the distance of the radius. Because both lever arms are equal, the forces are equal too.
105935.m: A fixed pulley is a lever with two equal arms.

105936.q: Why do you need a little more force than the weight of the load on a real fixed pulley?
a: Because of friction in the bearing and rope
Because the pulley makes the load heavier
Because gravity is stronger up there
Because the rope pushes air aside
105936.e: Friction arises in the axle and as the rope bends round the pulley. You have to make up for these losses with a little extra force.
105936.m: Friction makes every real pulley a little harder to use.

105937.q: In top-rope climbing, the rope runs through an anchor at the top of the rock and back down to the belayer. How does this anchor act?
105937.e: The anchor is fixed firmly to the rock and only changes the direction of the rope. That is what a fixed pulley does.
105937.m: A fixed redirect changes the direction, not the size, of the force.

105938.q: A load of 300 N hangs from a movable pulley. How big is the pulling force if the pulley's weight and friction are ignored?
105938.e: The load hangs on two sections of rope, each carrying half. 300 N divided by 2 gives 150 N.
105938.m: A movable pulley halves the force needed.

105939.q: A load is to be lifted 1 m with a movable pulley. How much rope do you have to pull?
105939.e: Both sections of rope beside the pulley must each get 1 m shorter. That is why you pull 2 m of rope in total.
105939.m: With a movable pulley you pull twice as much rope as the load rises.

105940.q: Why do you only need half the force with a movable pulley?
a: The load is shared between two sections of rope
The pulley lifts half by itself
The pulley makes the rope lighter
The Earth pulls the load less
105940.e: One end of the rope is fixed and you pull on the other. Both sections of rope carry the load together, so each carries half.
105940.m: Two supporting sections of rope share the load.

105941.q: A movable pulley weighs 20 N and the load 180 N. How big is the pulling force without friction?
105941.e: The movable pulley is lifted too, so its weight counts: 180 N plus 20 N gives 200 N. Divided by 2 sections of rope, that is 100 N.
105941.m: With a movable pulley you lift the pulley's weight as well.

105942.q: You pull the end of the rope of a movable pulley at 0.4 m/s. How fast does the load rise?
105942.e: The load covers only half the rope distance. So it also rises only half as fast: 0.4 m/s divided by 2 gives 0.2 m/s.
105942.m: On a movable pulley the load moves half as fast as the end of the rope.

105944.q: Why is a movable pulley often combined with a fixed pulley?
a: So that you can pull downwards
So that the load rises faster
So that you need less rope
105944.e: A movable pulley on its own needs an upward pull. An extra fixed pulley redirects the rope so you can pull down comfortably.
105944.m: An extra fixed pulley turns the direction of pull downwards.

105945.q: What happens to the force needed if the two sections of rope at a movable pulley run at a steep slant instead of vertically?
a: It becomes more than half the load
It becomes less than half the load
It stays exactly half the load
105945.e: With slanting ropes, only part of the rope force acts upwards. For the load still to be carried, the rope force has to get bigger.
105945.m: Vertical ropes make best use of the force on a movable pulley.

105946.q: A block and tackle carries a load of 1200 N on 6 sections of rope. How big is the pulling force without friction?
105946.e: The load is shared between 6 supporting sections of rope. 1200 N divided by 6 gives 200 N.
105946.m: With a block and tackle, divide the load by the number of supporting rope sections.

105947.q: A block and tackle has 3 movable pulleys in the lower block. How many supporting sections of rope does it have?
105947.e: Each movable pulley hangs on two sections of rope. With 3 movable pulleys that is 3 times 2, so 6 supporting sections.
105947.m: Each movable pulley adds two supporting sections of rope.

105948.q: A load is lifted 2 m with a block and tackle that has 5 supporting sections of rope. How much rope do you have to pull?
105948.e: Each of the 5 sections must get 2 m shorter. 5 times 2 m gives 10 m of rope.
105948.m: Rope distance is lifting height times the number of supporting sections.

105949.q: A crate with a mass of 80 kg hangs from a block and tackle with 4 supporting sections of rope. Roughly how big is the pulling force (g = 10 N/kg, no friction)?
105949.e: The weight is 80 kg times 10 N/kg, so 800 N. Divided by 4 sections of rope, this gives 200 N.
105949.m: First work out the weight, then divide by the rope sections.

105950.q: Which Greek scholar is said to have moved a loaded ship on his own using a block and tackle?
105950.e: The ancient writer Plutarch tells that Archimedes showed the power of pulleys in this way. Whether it happened exactly like that is not certain.
105950.m: According to legend, Archimedes showed the power of the block and tackle.

105951.q: In a compound pulley system with 3 movable pulleys, each pulley halves the force again. What fraction of the load is needed?
105951.e: Each movable pulley halves the force: a half times a half times a half gives an eighth. In return you pull eight times as much rope.
105951.m: In a compound pulley system each pulley halves the force again.

105952.q: Why do you need more than a quarter of the load on a real block and tackle with 4 sections of rope?
a: Friction and the weight of the lower pulleys are added
The ropes get heavier as you pull
The load gets heavier as it is lifted
The rope stretches and lifts too
105952.e: There is friction in every pulley, and the lower block is lifted too. That is why the force needed is above the ideal value.
105952.m: A real block and tackle needs more force than calculated because of friction.

105953.q: Where are blocks and tackles often used?
a: On sailing ships and building sites
105953.e: With a block and tackle you can lift heavy loads with little force. Sailors use them to hoist sails, and on building sites they lift materials.
105953.m: Blocks and tackles lift heavy loads with little force.

105954.q: Someone can pull with 150 N and uses a block and tackle with 4 supporting sections of rope. What is the largest load they can lift without friction?
105954.e: The pulling force is multiplied by the number of rope sections. 150 N times 4 gives 600 N.
105954.m: The lifting power of a block and tackle is pulling force times the number of supporting sections.

105955.q: A load of 500 N is pulled 2 m high up a 10 m long ramp. What force is needed without friction?
105955.e: Force is to load as height is to length. 500 N times 2 m divided by 10 m gives 100 N.
105955.m: The longer the ramp for the same height, the smaller the force.

105956.q: What does a road sign showing a “12%” gradient mean?
a: Over 100 m horizontally the road rises 12 m
Over 12 m the road rises 100 m
105956.e: The gradient in per cent tells you how many metres of height are gained over 100 m of horizontal distance. So 12% means 12 m in 100 m.
105956.m: A percentage gradient means metres of height per 100 m horizontally.

105957.q: Why are wheelchair ramps built with only a gentle slope?
a: So that you can go up them with little force
So that the wheelchair goes faster
So that the ramp takes up less space
So that the wheels do not get wet
105957.e: A gentle ramp is a long inclined plane. The smaller the slope, the smaller the downhill force you have to overcome going up. In return, the ramp needs more space.
105957.m: Gentle ramps need little force but a lot of space.

105958.q: What angle is a gradient of 100 per cent equal to?
105958.e: At 100% you rise exactly 100 m over 100 m horizontally. Height and horizontal distance are equal, which gives an angle of 45 degrees.
105958.m: A gradient of one hundred per cent is 45 degrees.

105959.q: A ramp is built twice as long for the same height. How does the force needed change without friction?
105959.e: The force is inversely proportional to the length of the ramp. Twice the length for the same height means half the force.
105959.m: Twice the ramp length means half the force.

105960.q: What is the component of force that pulls an object down an inclined plane called?
105960.e: Weight can be split into two parts. The part parallel to the slope is called the downhill force and pulls the object down.
105960.m: The downhill force pulls an object down the slope.

105961.q: What is the component of force with which an object presses at right angles onto the surface of an inclined plane called?
105961.e: At right angles to the surface acts the normal force. The steeper the slope, the smaller it becomes.
105961.m: The normal force presses at right angles onto the surface.

105962.q: What does the golden rule of mechanics say, more or less?
a: What you save in force, you must make up in distance
What you save in distance, you also save in force
Every machine saves force and distance at the same time
Force and distance are always equal
105962.e: Simple machines can reduce the force needed. In return, the distance becomes longer in the same proportion.
105962.m: What is saved in force must be added in distance.

105963.q: According to the golden rule, which quantity stays the same in a frictionless simple machine?
105963.e: Work is force times distance. If the force gets smaller, the distance gets bigger, and the product stays the same.
105963.m: Simple machines do not save work.

105964.q: How much work is needed without friction to lift a load of 500 N by 2 m?
105964.e: Work is force times distance: 500 N times 2 m gives 1000 joules. This is true with or without a machine.
105964.m: Work done lifting is weight times height.

105965.q: A 300 N crate is pushed 1.5 m high up a 6 m ramp. What force is needed without friction?
105965.e: The work of lifting is 300 N times 1.5 m, so 450 J. This work is spread over 6 m: 450 J divided by 6 m gives 75 N.
105965.m: The same work over a longer distance needs less force.

105966.q: In which unit is work measured?
105966.e: The unit of work is the joule, named after the physicist James Prescott Joule. The newton is the unit of force, the watt the unit of power.

105967.e: One joule is the work done by a force of 1 newton along a distance of 1 metre.
105967.m: One joule is one newton metre.

105968.q: Which basic law of physics lies behind the golden rule of mechanics?
a: The law of conservation of energy
105968.e: Energy can be neither created nor destroyed. So a machine cannot give out more work than you put in.
105968.m: No machine creates energy out of nothing.

105969.q: How does friction change the work you have to put into a simple machine?
a: You have to put in more work
You have to put in less work
The work stays exactly the same
105969.e: Part of the work put in is turned into heat by friction. That is why you have to put in more work than reaches the load.
105969.m: Friction costs extra work in every machine.

105970.q: With a block and tackle you lift 400 N by 3 m and pull with 100 N. How much rope do you have to pull without friction?
105970.e: The work on the load is 400 N times 3 m, so 1200 J. With 100 N you need 1200 J divided by 100 N, so 12 m.
105970.m: A quarter of the force means four times the distance.

105971.q: Which simple machine can you imagine a wedge to be made from?
105971.e: A wedge is made of two inclined planes placed back to back. Instead of pushing the load up, you push the planes into the material.
105971.m: A wedge is made of two inclined planes.

105972.q: Why does a slim wedge split wood with less force than a thick wedge of the same length?
a: It is longer in relation to the width of its back
It is made of harder wood
It turns as it goes in
105972.e: The longer the wedge is compared with the width of its back, the more the striking force is turned into splitting force. In return it has to go in further.
105972.m: A slim wedge multiplies force more than a thick one.

105973.q: In which direction does a wedge mainly redirect the force of a blow?
a: Sideways, across the direction of the blow
Exactly in the direction of the blow
105973.e: The blow drives the wedge forwards. Its slanting sides push the material apart sideways.
105973.m: A wedge turns a blow into sideways forces.

105974.q: Which tool used by stone sculptors works as a wedge?
105974.e: The blade of a chisel is wedge-shaped. When you strike it with a mallet, it splits pieces off the stone.
105974.m: A chisel works like a wedge.

105975.q: Which farm implement cuts and turns the soil with a wedge-shaped share?
105975.e: The ploughshare cuts into the ground like a wedge and lifts the layer of soil. The mouldboard then turns it over.
105975.m: The ploughshare goes into the ground like a wedge.

105976.q: Which parts of a pair of scissors act as wedges?
105976.e: Each blade has a wedge-shaped ground edge. This lets the blades go into the material and cut it.
105976.m: The blades of scissors are narrow wedges.

105977.q: A wedge is driven 4 cm into wood with 100 N and pushes the wood 1 cm apart. How big is the splitting force without friction, according to the golden rule?
105977.e: The work stays the same: 100 N times 4 cm must equal splitting force times 1 cm. That gives 400 N.
105977.m: A long distance travelled by the wedge creates a large splitting force.

105978.q: What is the distance a screw moves forward in one complete turn called?
105978.e: The pitch is the distance between two neighbouring threads. The screw goes in by exactly that much with each turn.
105978.m: With each turn a screw moves forward by one pitch.

105979.q: A screw has a pitch of 1.5 mm. How far does it go in after 20 turns?
105979.e: It goes in 1.5 mm per turn. 20 times 1.5 mm gives 30 mm.
105979.m: Depth is pitch times the number of turns.

105980.q: What is the advantage of a thread with a small pitch?
a: You need less force but more turns
You need more force but fewer turns
You need less force and fewer turns
105980.e: A fine thread is a gentle inclined plane. The force needed is smaller, but you have to turn it more often.
105980.m: A fine thread saves force but costs turns.

105981.q: Which device for lifting a car uses a threaded spindle?
105981.e: With a scissor jack you turn a threaded spindle. Thanks to the thread, a small force on the crank is enough to lift a car.
105981.m: A scissor jack lifts the car with a thread.

105982.q: Which device on a workbench clamps work pieces with great force using a threaded spindle?
105982.e: In a vice a spindle presses the jaws together. The lever on the handle and the thread greatly increase the force.
105982.m: A vice clamps tight with a thread and a lever.

105983.q: Which part of a bike has a left-hand thread so that it does not come loose when you pedal?
105983.e: With a right-hand thread the left pedal would slowly loosen as you pedal. With a left-hand thread it tightens instead.
105983.m: The left bike pedal has a left-hand thread.

105984.q: Why does a tightened screw not turn back out by itself under load?
a: Friction in the thread holds it
The screw head is too heavy
105984.e: With ordinary threads the pitch is so gentle that friction is bigger than the force that would turn the screw back. This is called self-locking.
105984.m: Self-locking through friction holds screws in place.

105985.q: Which measuring instrument uses a fine screw to measure lengths to a hundredth of a millimetre?
105985.e: In a micrometer the spindle moves only by a small pitch per turn. A scale on the thimble divides this turn finely.
105985.m: A fine screw lets you measure very precisely.

105986.q: What is a wheel and axle?
a: A wheel and an axle fixed together on the same shaft
A wheel that floats on waves
Two gear wheels with a chain
105986.e: In a wheel and axle, a large wheel or crank and a thinner axle are rigidly joined. They both turn together.
105986.m: In a wheel and axle, the wheel and axle turn together.

105987.q: A wheel and axle has a wheel with a 30 cm radius and an axle with a 5 cm radius. A load of 600 N hangs from the axle. What force is needed on the wheel?
105987.e: Force times wheel radius equals load times axle radius. 600 N times 5 cm divided by 30 cm gives 100 N.
105987.m: A large wheel on a thin axle saves force.

105988.q: Above old wells you often see a crank that winds a rope onto an axle. What is it for?
a: To pull up the full bucket with little force
105988.e: The crank and axle form a wheel and axle. The hand moves round a large circle and the axle round only a small one. So you need less force to bring up the bucket.
105988.m: A crank with an axle is a wheel and axle and saves force.

105989.q: Why did old lorries without power steering have especially large steering wheels?
a: A large radius reduces the force needed
You can see the road better
105989.e: The steering wheel is a wheel and axle. The bigger its radius, the smaller the force needed to turn the steering column.
105989.m: A large steering wheel needs less force.

105990.q: Why is a door handle easier to push down if you hold it at the outer end?
a: The lever arm to the axis is longer there
105990.e: The door handle turns about an axis like a wheel and axle. The further out you push, the bigger the turning effect for the same force.
105990.m: A long lever arm makes turning easier.

105991.q: Why does a screwdriver have a thick handle?
a: The large radius of the handle increases the turning effect
It stops it rolling off the table
105991.e: The handle and blade form a wheel and axle. The thick handle acts as a large wheel and the narrow blade as the axle, so the turning effect is increased.
105991.m: The thick handle turns the screwdriver into a wheel and axle.

105992.q: A crank has a radius of 40 cm and the rope axle 4 cm. How far does the hand move when the load is lifted 1 m?
105992.e: The ratio of the radii is 40 cm to 4 cm, so 10 to 1. The hand therefore covers ten times the distance: 10 m.
105992.m: With a wheel and axle you pay for the small force with a long distance.

105993.q: Which quantity is the same at the wheel and the axle when they are in balance?
105993.e: The moment is force times lever arm. In balance it is the same at the wheel and the axle, even though the forces are different.
105993.m: In balance the moments at the wheel and the axle are equal.

105994.q: On a bike a small sprocket is fixed to the large rear wheel. What do you gain from this?
a: Force and speed at the same time
105994.e: Here the force acts on the small axle and the large wheel moves. The rim of the wheel covers a much longer distance, but more force is needed for it.
105994.m: If a wheel and axle is driven at the axle, you gain speed.

105995.q: A driving gear with 36 teeth turns at 10 revolutions per minute and drives a gear with 12 teeth. How fast does the small gear turn?
105995.e: The ratio of teeth is 36 to 12, so 3 to 1. The small gear turns three times as fast: 10 times 3 gives 30 revolutions per minute.
105995.m: The gear with fewer teeth turns faster.

105996.q: A driving gear with 15 teeth drives a gear with 45 teeth. What do you gain at the large gear?
a: Three times the turning effect at a third of the speed
Three times the speed at a third of the turning effect
Three times the speed and three times the turning effect
105996.e: The large gear turns three times more slowly. In return, its turning effect, the moment, is three times as big.
105996.m: Gears that turn more slowly deliver more moment.

105997.q: What is a gear ratio called where the driven gear turns faster than the driving gear?
105997.e: If a large gear drives a small one, the small one turns faster. This is called gearing up.
105997.m: A large gear driving a small one gears up.

105998.q: Why is an idler gear put between two gear wheels?
a: So that both wheels turn in the same direction
So that the gear ratio doubles
So that the gearbox is quieter
So that the teeth do not wear
105998.e: Two gears that mesh directly turn in opposite directions. An idler gear reverses the direction once more but does not change the ratio.
105998.m: An idler gear changes the direction, not the ratio.

105999.q: Gear A (40 teeth) drives gear B (20 teeth), and gear B drives gear C (10 teeth). How many times does C turn when A turns once?
105999.e: B has half as many teeth as A and turns twice. C has half as many teeth as B and turns twice as often, so 4 times.
105999.m: The ratios of gears in a row are multiplied.

106000.q: What must two gear wheels have in common to mesh smoothly?
106000.e: The teeth of both wheels must be the same size and the same distance apart. Engineers call this the same module.
106000.m: Gears only mesh properly if their teeth are the same size.

106001.q: In a clock, in what ratio do the minute hand and the hour hand turn?
106001.e: The minute hand turns once in an hour and the hour hand once in 12 hours. So the hand gearing has a ratio of 12 to 1.
106001.m: The minute hand turns twelve times faster than the hour hand.

106002.q: A motor turns at 3000 revolutions per minute. Its gear with 10 teeth drives a gear with 50 teeth. How fast does this gear turn?
106002.e: The large gear has 5 times as many teeth and so turns 5 times more slowly. 3000 divided by 5 gives 600.
106002.m: More teeth on the driven gear means fewer revolutions.

106003.q: Which gears are used to turn a rotation through 90 degrees?
106003.e: Bevel gears have slanted teeth on a cone-shaped surface. This lets two shafts be connected at right angles, for example in a hand drill.
106003.m: Bevel gears send rotation round the corner.

106004.q: Which type of gear is found in the tuning pegs of a guitar?
106004.e: A worm drives a gear on the string post. The gear reduces strongly, so the string can be tuned finely, and the string tension cannot turn it back.
106004.m: Guitar tuning pegs use a worm gear.

106005.q: Why does a car need a differential?
a: So the driving wheels can turn at different speeds in bends
So the engine runs more quietly
106005.e: On a bend the outer wheel covers a longer distance than the inner one. The differential shares the force so both wheels can turn at different speeds.
106005.m: The differential lets the wheels turn at different speeds in bends.

106006.q: What is the gear in the middle of a planetary gear system called?
106006.e: In a planetary gear system, planet gears circle round the central sun gear. On the outside they are surrounded by a ring gear with teeth on the inside.
106006.m: In a planetary gear system the planet gears circle the sun gear.

106007.q: Why do you pull away in first gear in a car with a manual gearbox?
a: It gives a lot of turning force at low speed
It saves the most petrol at high speed
It is kind to the brakes
106007.e: First gear reduces strongly: the engine turns fast and the wheels slowly, but with great force. You need this to get the stationary car moving.
106007.m: First gear gives a lot of force for pulling away.

106008.q: Which gear turns a rotation into a straight-line motion?
a: Two spur gears of the same size
