106724.m: For pressure, the force at right angles to the surface is what counts.

106725.q: A force of 2000 N produces a pressure of 4000 Pa. How big is the area?
106725.e: The area is force divided by pressure. 2000 N divided by 4000 Pa gives 0.5 m².
106725.m: If you know the force and pressure, divide the force by the pressure to get the area.

106726.e: One pascal is the pressure a force of 1 N exerts on an area of 1 m². That is a very small pressure.
106726.m: One pascal equals one newton per square metre.

106727.q: What did Blaise Pascal, after whom the unit of pressure is named, study?
106727.e: Pascal had measurements made showing that air pressure on a mountain is lower than in the valley. He also studied pressure in liquids.
106727.m: The pascal honours the scientist Blaise Pascal.

106728.q: In which century did Blaise Pascal live?
106728.e: Blaise Pascal lived from 1623 to 1662. So he belongs to the 17th century.
106728.m: Blaise Pascal lived in the 17th century.

106729.q: Which machine did Blaise Pascal build as a young man?
106729.e: Pascal built a calculating machine called the Pascaline. It helped his father, a tax official, to calculate faster.
106729.m: Blaise Pascal invented an early calculating machine.

106730.q: How many pascals are in 1 hectopascal?
106730.e: The prefix hecto means a hundred. So 1 hPa is 100 Pa.
106730.m: One hectopascal is a hundred pascals.

106731.q: How many pascals are in 1 kilopascal?
106731.e: Kilo means a thousand, as in kilometre or kilogram. So 1 kPa is 1000 Pa.
106731.m: One kilopascal is a thousand pascals.

106732.q: How many pascals are in 1 megapascal?
106732.e: Mega means a million. So 1 MPa is a million pascals; the strength of concrete or steel, for example, is given in megapascals.
106732.m: One megapascal is a million pascals.

106733.q: Which pressure is roughly the pressure of a sheet of paper lying flat on a table?
106733.e: A sheet of paper one square metre in size weighs less than one newton. So it presses on the table with about one pascal.
106733.m: One pascal is a very small pressure.

106734.q: How many pascals are in 1 bar?
106734.e: One bar is defined as exactly 100,000 Pa. That is roughly the air pressure at sea level.
106734.m: One bar is a hundred thousand pascals.

106735.q: How many hectopascals are in 1 bar?
106735.e: 1 bar is 100,000 Pa. Dividing by 100 gives 1000 hPa.
106735.m: One bar is a thousand hectopascals.

106736.e: Milli means one thousandth. So 1000 millibars make exactly 1 bar.
106736.m: A thousand millibars make one bar.

106737.q: Which unit is 1 millibar exactly equal to?
106737.e: 1 mbar is one thousandth of 100,000 Pa, so 100 Pa. That is exactly 1 hPa.
106737.m: A millibar is the same as a hectopascal.

106738.q: A bike tyre is pumped up to 4 bar above air pressure. How many kilopascals is that?
106738.e: 1 bar is 100,000 Pa, so 100 kPa. 4 times 100 kPa gives 400 kPa.
106738.m: One bar is a hundred kilopascals.

106739.q: Where do you often come across the unit bar in everyday life?
106739.e: At the petrol station you pump tyres up to 2.5 bar, for example. The bar is a unit of pressure.
106739.m: Tyre pressure is usually given in bar.

106740.q: Roughly what is the air pressure at sea level?
106740.e: At sea level the average air pressure is 1013 hPa. That is roughly 1 bar.
106740.m: At sea level the air pressure is about 1 bar.

106741.e: 1 bar is 100,000 Pa. 2.5 times 100,000 Pa gives 250,000 Pa.
106741.m: To convert bar into pascals, multiply by a hundred thousand.

106742.q: What pressure is a full compressed air cylinder for scuba divers typically filled to?
106742.e: Diving cylinders are usually filled to 200 bar, some to 300 bar. This fits a lot of air into a small cylinder.
106742.m: A diving cylinder holds air at very high pressure.

106743.q: How does the pressure change when a weight stands on a larger contact area?
106743.e: The same weight is spread over more area. So less force presses on each square metre.
106743.m: A large contact area reduces the pressure.

106744.q: Why do heavy lorries have lots of wheels?
a: The weight is spread over a bigger area.
They use less petrol that way.
106744.e: Many wheels increase the total contact area. So the pressure on the road is smaller and the surface is damaged less.
106744.m: Many wheels spare the road because the pressure is smaller.

106745.q: Why can narrow stiletto heels damage a wooden floor?
a: The small area creates a high pressure.
106745.e: With a stiletto, a large part of the body's weight rests on a tiny heel area. This creates a very high pressure that can leave dents in the wood.
106745.m: A narrow heel creates a high pressure on the floor.

106746.q: Why does a piste basher have wide caterpillar tracks instead of wheels?
a: So that it does not sink into the snow
106746.e: The wide tracks give a very large contact area. The pressure on the snow stays small, even though the vehicle weighs many tonnes.
106746.m: Wide caterpillar tracks stop it sinking into the snow.

106747.q: A brick with a weight of 30 N lies on an area of 0.02 m². How big is the pressure?
106747.e: Pressure is force divided by area. 30 N divided by 0.02 m² gives 1500 Pa.
106747.m: Pressure is calculated as force per area.

106748.q: On which side must you stand a brick for it to exert the greatest pressure on the ground?
a: It is the same on every side.
106748.e: The brick's weight always stays the same. So when it stands on its smallest face, the pressure is greatest.
106748.m: The smallest contact area gives the greatest pressure.

106749.q: Why do good rucksacks have wide shoulder straps?
a: They spread the load and press less.
They keep rain out of the rucksack.
106749.e: Wide straps rest on the shoulder with a bigger area. So the pressure is smaller and the straps dig in less.
106749.m: Wide straps press less on the shoulders.

106750.q: How should you move if you have fallen through thin ice and want to get yourself out?
a: Lying flat to spread your weight
106750.e: Lying down spreads the body's weight over a large area. The pressure on the ice gets smaller, and it is less likely to break.
106750.m: On thin ice you spread your weight by lying flat.

106751.q: Why does a house stand on a wide foundation?
a: So that it does not sink into the ground
106751.e: The foundation spreads the great weight of the house over a wide area. So the pressure on the ground is small enough.
106751.m: A wide foundation spreads the weight of a house.

106752.q: A person weighing 600 N stands in the snow in winter boots with a total sole area of 0.04 m². How big is the pressure?
106752.e: Pressure is force divided by area. 600 N divided by 0.04 m² gives 15,000 Pa.
106752.m: Small soles create a large pressure on the snow.

106753.q: The same person weighing 600 N wears snowshoes with a total area of 0.3 m². How big is the pressure now?
106753.e: 600 N divided by 0.3 m² gives 2000 Pa. The pressure is much smaller than with ordinary shoes.
106753.m: With snowshoes the pressure on the snow drops sharply.

106754.q: What is the fold-up climbing bar under the heel of modern snowshoes for?
a: It takes strain off the calves on steep climbs.
It reduces the pressure on the snow.
It acts as a brake going downhill.
It measures the angle of the slope.
106754.e: The climbing bar raises the heel so that the foot stays almost level on steep ground. This spares the calf muscles on the way up.
106754.m: A climbing bar makes steep climbs easier on snowshoes.

106755.q: What are the spikes or claws under modern snowshoes for?
a: For grip on hard or icy snow
106755.e: The claws grip hard snow and ice. So you slip less on steep sections.
106755.m: Claws under a snowshoe give grip on hard snow.

106756.q: What should snowshoers in Switzerland respect to protect animals?
106756.e: In wildlife rest areas, wild animals should be left undisturbed in winter. Every escape costs them a lot of energy that they can hardly replace in winter.
106756.m: Snowshoers avoid wildlife rest areas to spare wild animals.

106757.q: Which Alpine animal has wide, very hairy hind feet that act like snowshoes?
106757.e: The mountain hare has large, thickly furred hind feet. They spread its weight so that it hardly sinks into the snow.
106757.m: The mountain hare wears its snowshoes on its feet.

106758.q: What were traditional snowshoes usually made of?
a: A wooden frame with a web of straps
A single piece of sheet iron
106758.e: Traditional snowshoes had a bent wooden frame. A net of leather or rawhide straps was stretched inside it.
106758.m: In the past, snowshoes were made of wood and leather straps.

106759.q: Why do you sink in deeper on snowshoes when you carry a heavy rucksack?
a: The weight is greater, but the area stays the same.
The area of the snowshoes gets smaller.
The rucksack makes the snow warmer.
106759.e: With the rucksack, a bigger force presses on the same area. So the pressure on the snow rises.
106759.m: More weight on the same area increases the pressure.

106760.q: Why can you lie on a bed of nails with lots of nails without getting hurt?
a: The weight is spread over a great many points.
The nails are made of rubber.
106760.e: Each single nail carries only a small part of the body's weight. The pressure per point stays so small that the skin is not pierced.
106760.m: Many nails share the weight and reduce the pressure per nail.

106761.q: A person weighing 600 N lies evenly on 600 nails. What force acts on a single nail?
106761.e: 600 N divided by 600 nails gives 1 N per nail. That is about the weight of a 100 g bar of chocolate.
106761.m: The force per nail is the weight divided by the number of nails.

106762.q: A force of 500 N is spread over 1000 nail points, each with an area of 1 mm². How big is the pressure?
106762.e: 1000 points of 1 mm² each make 1000 mm², so 0.001 m². 500 N divided by 0.001 m² gives 500,000 Pa.
106762.m: Very small areas quickly lead to very large pressures.

106763.q: What are performers called who lie on a bed of nails as a show?
106763.e: Fakirs perform feats such as lying on beds of nails. The word comes from the Arabic faqir, meaning poor.
106763.m: Someone who lies on a bed of nails is called a fakir.

106764.q: Why would it be dangerous to lie on a board with only a few nails?
a: Each nail would have to carry much more weight.
A few nails are always blunt.
106764.e: With only a few nails, a large force acts on each point. The pressure becomes so high that the nails go into the skin.
106764.m: The fewer the nails, the higher the pressure on each point.

106765.q: Why does it hurt so much to step barefoot on a small toy building brick?
a: Your whole weight presses on a tiny area.
Your foot is especially cold there.
106765.e: The body's weight suddenly acts on the small edges and studs of the brick. This creates a very high pressure on the sole of the foot.
106765.m: A small area under your foot creates a high pressure.

106766.q: Why must all the nails on a bed of nails be exactly the same height?
a: Otherwise a few nails carry all the weight.
Otherwise the board is too heavy.
Otherwise the nails do not shine.
106766.e: If some nails stick up higher, the body first rests only on them. These few points would then have to carry the whole load.
106766.m: Nails of the same height spread the weight evenly.

106767.q: How does the pressure on the soles of your feet change if you stand on the bed of nails instead of lying on it?
106767.e: Standing, your whole weight rests on the few nails under your feet. Lying down, it is spread over many more nails.
106767.m: Standing on a bed of nails gives more pressure than lying on it.

106768.q: Why does a drawing pin have a wide head and a fine point?
a: There is little pressure on the thumb and a lot at the point.
106768.e: The force of the thumb is the same at the head and the point. On the wide head the pressure is small, but on the tiny point it is huge.
106768.m: With a drawing pin, the wide head spares your thumb and the point goes in.

106769.q: A knife edge is 10 cm long and 0.1 mm wide. What pressure is produced if you press with 20 N?
106769.e: The area is 100 mm times 0.1 mm, so 10 mm² or 0.00001 m². 20 N divided by 0.00001 m² gives 2,000,000 Pa.
106769.m: A thin edge creates enormous pressure even with little force.

106770.q: Why do you have to press harder with a blunt knife?
a: The edge is wider, so the pressure is smaller.
106770.e: A worn edge is wider and rounded. So more force is needed for the same pressure.
106770.m: A wide edge needs more force for the same pressure.

106771.q: Why are the blades of ice skates so narrow?
a: They create a high pressure on the ice.
They are easier to carry that way.
So that the ice does not melt.
So that you skate more slowly.
106771.e: The narrow blade presses the body's weight onto a small area. Thanks to the high pressure it grips the ice well and can be steered.
106771.m: Narrow blades create a high pressure on the ice.

106772.q: What does sharpening a knife do?
106772.e: When sharpening, material is removed from the edge until it is very thin again. The force then acts on a smaller area again.
106772.m: Sharpening makes the edge narrow again and the knife sharp.

106773.q: Why is a hypodermic needle ground at a slant?
a: Its fine point goes in with little force.
So that it holds more liquid.
So that it does not rust.
So that it is easier to see.
106773.e: The slanted grind creates a very fine point. A high pressure acts on it, so the needle slides easily through the skin.
106773.m: A fine point goes in with little force.

106774.q: Why can you cut a wheel of cheese with a thin wire?
a: The thin wire creates a high pressure.
106774.e: The wire is very thin and so presses on a tiny area. The high pressure cuts the cheese cleanly without it crumbling.
106774.m: A thin wire cuts thanks to high pressure.

106775.q: What does hydraulics use to transmit forces?
106775.e: In hydraulics, pressure is applied to a liquid. The liquid passes the pressure on through pipes and moves a piston somewhere else.

106776.q: Which property of liquids makes hydraulics possible?
106776.e: A liquid hardly gives way when pressed because it can scarcely be compressed. So the pressure arrives in full at the other end.

106777.q: Which part of a car usually works hydraulically?
106777.e: When you press the brake pedal, brake fluid is put under pressure. This pressure presses the brake pads on at all the wheels.
106777.m: A car's brakes work with brake fluid.

106778.q: How are the arms of a large excavator usually moved?
106778.e: In the hydraulic cylinders, oil presses on pistons. These move the boom and bucket with great force.
106778.m: Excavators move their arms with hydraulic cylinders.

106779.q: Which liquid is usually used in hydraulic machines?
106779.e: Hydraulic oil can hardly be compressed and also lubricates the moving parts. It protects against rust too.
106779.m: Oil usually flows in hydraulic systems.

106780.q: Why is air in a hydraulic brake line dangerous?
a: Air can be compressed, so the brake feels spongy.
Air makes the brake too strong.
Air sets the brake fluid on fire.
106780.e: Air bubbles are squashed when braking instead of passing on the pressure. The pedal feels spongy and the braking effect drops.
106780.m: Air in the brake line weakens the brakes.

106781.q: Which Greek word does the term hydraulics come from?
106781.e: Hydor means water in Greek. The first hydraulic devices really did work with water.
106781.m: Hydraulics comes from the Greek word for water.

106782.q: What is often used in a car workshop to lift a whole car up?
a: A block and tackle made of string
106782.e: A hydraulic lift uses oil to press on pistons that raise the car. This lets you work comfortably underneath the vehicle.
106782.m: Workshop lifts raise cars using hydraulics.

106783.q: What is the force multiplication of a hydraulic press based on?
106783.e: The pressure is the same throughout the liquid. On the large piston it acts on more area and so produces a bigger force.
106783.m: A hydraulic press multiplies forces with two pistons of different sizes.

106784.q: The small piston of a hydraulic press has an area of 10 cm², the large one 200 cm². You press with 50 N. What force is produced at the large piston?
106784.e: The large piston is 200 divided by 10, so 20 times bigger. So the force is 20 times bigger: 50 N times 20 gives 1000 N.
106784.m: The force grows in the same proportion as the piston area.

106785.q: A hydraulic press has pistons of 5 cm² and 100 cm². How much force is needed on the small piston for 2000 N at the large one?
106785.e: The large piston is 100 divided by 5, so 20 times bigger. 2000 N divided by 20 gives 100 N.
106785.m: The small piston needs less force by the same factor that its area is smaller.

106786.q: What is the price paid for the gain in force with a hydraulic press?
a: The small piston has to travel a much longer distance.
106786.e: The liquid pushed out by the small piston spreads over a much larger area under the large piston. That is why the large piston only moves a short way.
106786.m: A gain in force is paid for with a longer distance.

106787.q: The large piston of a press is 20 times bigger than the small one. The small piston is pushed down 20 cm. How far does the large one rise?
106787.e: The volume of liquid pushed aside is the same on both sides. With 20 times the area, the large piston moves only 20 cm divided by 20, so 1 cm.
106787.m: The large piston moves less by the same factor that it is bigger.

106788.q: What is a hydraulic press used for in industry, for example?
a: Shaping sheet metal for car parts
106788.e: A hydraulic press produces very large forces. It is used, for example, to press sheet metal into the shape of car doors.
106788.m: Hydraulic presses produce very large forces.

106789.q: Which tool uses the principle of the hydraulic press to lift a car when changing a wheel?
106789.e: With a hydraulic jack you use a small piston to pump oil under a large piston. This lets you lift a heavy car with little force.
106789.m: A hydraulic jack lifts a whole car with little force.

106790.q: How big is the pressure in the liquid under the small piston compared with the large piston?
106790.e: In a liquid that is enclosed and at rest, pressure spreads equally everywhere. Only the forces on the pistons are different.
106790.m: In the press the pressure is the same everywhere.

106791.q: At a depth of 10 m, with what force does the water press on an area of 1 m² in addition to air pressure?
106791.e: At a depth of 10 m the water pressure is about 1 bar, so 100,000 Pa. Force is pressure times area: 100,000 Pa times 1 m² gives about 100,000 N.
106791.m: You get the force on an area by multiplying the pressure by the area.

106792.q: Water squirts out of a bottle with three holes one above the other. From which hole does the water come out fastest?
106792.e: Above the lowest hole there is the tallest column of water. The pressure is greatest there, and the water squirts furthest.
106792.m: Water pressure is greatest at the bottom of a container.

106793.q: What does the water pressure at the bottom of a container depend on?
a: The height of the water above the bottom
106793.e: The pressure at the bottom depends only on the height of the column of water, not on the shape. This is called the hydrostatic paradox.
106793.m: The pressure at the bottom depends only on the height of the water.

106794.q: How does a gravity dam withstand the water pressure of the reservoir?
a: Through cables to the mountain tops
106794.e: A gravity dam is so heavy that the water can neither push it away nor tip it over. That is why it is very wide at the bottom and made of huge amounts of concrete.
106794.m: A gravity dam resists the water through its weight.

106795.q: Why do water towers or reservoirs often stand high above a village?
a: So that the water flows into the houses with enough pressure
So that the water stays cooler
So that you can see them from far away
So that birds can bathe in them
106795.e: The higher the water stands above the houses, the greater the water pressure in the pipes. So it flows out of the tap without a pump.
106795.m: Reservoirs high up give water pressure in the pipes.

106796.q: Where is the water pressure at a depth of 10 m slightly greater, in the sea or in a mountain lake?
106796.e: Salt water has a higher density than fresh water. A column of seawater of the same height is therefore heavier and presses harder.
106796.m: At the same depth, salt water creates slightly more pressure than fresh water.

106797.q: Roughly how much water pressure is added to the air pressure at a depth of 25 m?
106797.e: For every 10 m of depth the pressure rises by about 1 bar. 25 m divided by 10 m gives about 2.5 bar.
106797.m: You estimate water pressure by dividing the depth in metres by ten.

106798.q: Roughly what is the total pressure at a depth of 10 m if you include air pressure?
106798.e: At the surface there is about 1 bar of air pressure. At 10 m depth about 1 bar of water pressure is added, making about 2 bar in total.
106798.m: At ten metres deep, the pressure is about double that at the surface.

106799.q: Roughly what is the total pressure at a diving depth of 30 m?
106799.e: 30 m of water give about 3 bar of water pressure. Add 1 bar of air pressure, making about 4 bar in total.
106799.m: Always add the air pressure to the water pressure.

106800.q: Roughly what is the water pressure at the deepest point of the ocean, about 11 km down?
106800.e: For every 10 m of depth the pressure rises by about 1 bar. 11,000 m divided by 10 gives about 1100 bar.
106800.m: In the deep sea there is enormous water pressure.

106801.q: Why does a submarine have a very thick, strong hull?
a: So that it can withstand the water pressure at depth
So that it floats more easily
106801.e: At great depth the water presses with enormous force on every part of the hull. A weak hull would be crushed.
106801.m: The thick hull protects a submarine from the water pressure.

106802.q: A balloon filled with air is taken from the surface down to a depth of 20 m. Roughly how does its volume change?
a: It becomes about a third as big.
It becomes about twice as big.
It becomes about a twentieth as big.
106802.e: At 20 m depth the total pressure is about three times as big as at the surface. So the air in the balloon is squashed to about a third.
106802.m: Air is squashed more the deeper you go.

106803.q: How does a dive computer measure the current diving depth?
a: From the colour of the water
106803.e: A pressure sensor in the dive computer measures the pressure of the surrounding water. The device works out the depth from this.
106803.m: A dive computer finds the depth from the water pressure.

106804.q: What is diving on a single breath, without breathing equipment, called?
106804.e: In freediving, also called apnoea diving, divers hold their breath. Apnoea means stopping breathing.
106804.m: In freediving you dive on just one breath.

106805.q: Why are deep-sea fish not crushed by the huge water pressure?
a: The pressure inside their bodies is the same as outside.
There is no pressure in the deep sea.
106805.e: Deep-sea fish have no large air-filled spaces. Their bodies are made mostly of water, so the pressure is the same inside and out.
106805.m: Deep-sea fish can stand the pressure because it is the same inside and out.

106806.q: How do many divers equalise the pressure in their ears as they go down?
a: Pinch the nose and gently breathe out against it
106806.e: Gently pushing against the closed nose lets air into the middle ear. This adjusts the pressure in the middle ear to the water pressure.
106806.m: When diving, you equalise ear pressure by pinching your nose.

106807.q: What helps against pressure in the ears when a plane is landing?
a: Holding your breath for a long time
106807.e: Swallowing and yawning briefly open the connection between the throat and the middle ear. This equalises the pressure.
106807.m: Swallowing and yawning help to equalise the pressure in your ears.

106808.q: Which tube connects the middle ear with the throat and makes pressure equalisation possible?
106808.e: The Eustachian tube runs from the middle ear to the throat. Air can flow through it into the middle ear.
106808.m: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear and the throat.

106809.q: Why can you breathe normally in an airliner at a height of 10 km?
a: Outside there is normal air pressure up there.
106809.e: At great height the air pressure outside is far too low. So the cabin is brought to a higher pressure with compressed air, about the same as in the mountains at a height of 2000 to 2500 m.
106809.m: The pressurised cabin protects people in the plane from the low air pressure.

106810.q: Which illness can a diver get if she comes up too fast after a deep dive?
106810.e: When surfacing quickly, the pressure drops too fast. Nitrogen dissolved in the blood then forms bubbles, rather like when you open a bottle of fizzy water.
106810.m: Coming up slowly protects against decompression sickness.

106811.q: Why does a sealed bag of crisps puff up when you take it up a high mountain?
a: Outside, the air pressure is lower than inside the bag.
106811.e: The bag was sealed in the valley at a higher air pressure. Up high the outside air presses less, so the air inside the bag expands.
106811.m: In the mountains, air in sealed packets expands.

106812.q: Which thin membrane in the ear bulges when the pressure on its two sides is different?
106812.e: The eardrum separates the ear canal from the middle ear. If the pressure on one side is greater, it is stretched and the ear feels blocked.
106812.m: A difference in pressure stretches the eardrum.

106813.q: Why should you not dive with a bad cold?
a: Swollen mucous membranes make it hard to equalise pressure.
The diving mask never steams up.
106813.e: With a cold, the mucous membranes swell and can block the connection to the middle ear. Then equalising the pressure does not work and the ear can be injured.
106813.m: With a cold, equalising the pressure often does not work.

106814.q: In Switzerland, how long does the apprenticeship as a forest worker (Forstwart EFZ) take?
106814.e: The basic vocational training takes three years and ends with the Federal VET Diploma (EFZ). Part of the training takes place in inter-company courses.
106814.m: The forest worker apprenticeship takes three years.

106815.q: Which tool does a forest worker use most often to fell trees?
106815.e: With the chainsaw the forest worker fells trees and cuts trunks to length. Using it safely is practised a lot during the apprenticeship.
106815.m: The chainsaw is the forest worker’s most important tool.

106816.q: Why does a forest worker wear chainsaw trousers?
a: They block the saw chain on contact
They protect against rain and snow
They keep your legs warm in winter
106816.e: The trousers contain long fibres that get pulled into the chain on contact and stop the saw in a flash. This prevents serious leg injuries.
106816.m: Chainsaw trousers stop the chainsaw chain in an accident.

106817.q: At what kind of school do people in Switzerland train further to become a forester (Förster HF)?
106817.e: The abbreviation HF stands for Höhere Fachschule, a college of higher education. The usual requirement is a forest worker apprenticeship and a few years of work experience.
106817.m: Foresters train further at a college of higher education.

106818.q: Why do forest workers in the mountains look after the protection forest?
a: It protects villages from avalanches and falling rocks
It makes room for ski runs
106818.e: A healthy mountain forest holds back snow and rocks. Forest workers make sure young trees keep growing there.
106818.m: Protection forest keeps villages safe from avalanches and falling rocks.

106819.q: What is the work called in which forest workers remove weak or troublesome saplings in a young forest?
106819.e: In young forest tending, forest workers help well-grown trees and remove their competitors. This creates a stable, mixed forest.
106819.m: Young forest tending helps the best young trees.

106820.q: Why do forest workers never work completely alone when felling trees?
a: So that someone can help if there is an accident
Because the noise law requires it
Because a chainsaw has two handles
So that the work goes faster
106820.e: Felling trees is one of the most dangerous jobs there is. If there is an accident, someone must be able to give first aid and raise the alarm straight away.
106820.m: For safety reasons you never work alone in the forest.

106821.q: Which headgear is part of a forest worker’s protective equipment?
a: Helmet with ear defenders and visor
Straw hat with a wide brim
106821.e: The forestry helmet protects against falling branches. Ear defenders and visor protect against the noise of the saw and flying chips.
106821.m: Forest workers wear a helmet with ear defenders and a visor.

106822.q: Why do you first saw a wedge-shaped cut into the trunk when felling a tree?
a: So that the tree falls in the direction you want
So that the tree grows faster
So that the resin can run out
So that birds can nest in it
106822.e: The wedge-shaped cut is called the felling notch. It is sawn on the side the tree should fall towards. Then the felling cut is made from the opposite side.
106822.m: The felling notch sets the direction in which the tree falls.

106823.q: Why do you not saw right through the trunk when felling a tree?
a: The strip of wood left standing guides the tree like a hinge
So that the tree can grow back later
Because otherwise the saw goes blunt
So that the tree grows more slowly
106823.e: The narrow strip of wood that is left standing is called the hinge. It works like a hinge and guides the falling trunk in the direction you want.
106823.m: The hinge guides the tree as it falls.

106824.q: In which season is most wood traditionally cut in Switzerland?
106824.e: In winter the sap in the tree is at rest, birds are not nesting, and frozen ground is less damaged by machines.
106824.m: Wood is traditionally cut in winter.

106825.q: In very steep terrain, what is often used to get felled trunks out of the forest?
106825.e: A cable crane pulls the trunks along a supporting cable over steep slopes to a road. In the Alps and foothills this is often the gentlest option.
106825.m: In steep forests a cable crane brings the wood out.

106826.q: What is the machine called that fells trees, strips off the branches and saws them into pieces?
106826.e: The harvester does all the steps with a single gripping head, just as its name suggests. It is used mainly on flat ground.
106826.m: A harvester is a timber harvesting machine.

106827.q: Why may timber harvesting machines only drive on fixed tracks in the forest?
a: So that the rest of the forest floor is not squashed
So that they do not drive too fast
So that hikers can see them better
So that they use less fuel
106827.e: The fixed tracks are called skid trails. If machines only drive there, the rest of the forest floor stays loose, and roots and soil creatures are protected.
106827.m: In the forest, machines only drive on skid trails.

106828.q: Which unit measures the volume of wood in logs without any air gaps?
106828.e: A solid cubic metre equals one cubic metre of solid wood. The timber harvest is measured in this unit.
106828.m: A solid cubic metre is one cubic metre of pure wood.

106829.q: What do you call removing the branches from a felled trunk?
106829.e: When delimbing, the branches are sawn off right at the trunk. Only after that is the trunk cut into pieces.
106829.m: Delimbing means removing the branches from the trunk.

106830.q: What is meant by natural regeneration in a forest?
a: Young trees grow from the seeds of old trees
Trees are cut back every year
106830.e: In natural regeneration, seeds from old trees fall to the ground and sprout there. People do not have to plant anything.
106830.m: In natural regeneration, the forest sows itself.

106831.q: What do young trees on the forest floor need most of all to grow well?
106831.e: That is why foresters thin out the forest on purpose. More sunlight reaches the ground through the gaps in the canopy.
106831.m: Young trees need light to grow.

106832.q: Which tree species, as a shade-tolerant tree, can grow up even under a dense canopy?
106832.e: Young silver firs can tolerate a lot of shade and can wait for decades under old trees until a gap opens.
106832.m: The silver fir grows well even in shade.

106833.q: Which tree species, as a pioneer, is often the first to grow on open land?
106833.e: Birches produce a great many light seeds that the wind carries far. In full sunlight they grow quickly.
106833.m: The birch is a typical pioneer tree species.

106834.q: What is typical of a selection forest (Plenterwald), like those found in the Emmental?
a: Young and old trees grow mixed side by side
All the trees are exactly the same age
The trees stand in straight rows
106834.e: In a selection forest, only single trees are ever harvested. That is why young and old trees stand side by side and the forest keeps renewing itself.
106834.m: In a selection forest, young and old trees stand side by side.

106835.q: Why is natural regeneration usually cheaper than planting?
a: You do not have to buy and plant young trees
The federal government pays for every seedling
You no longer need forestry staff
106835.e: In natural regeneration, the old trees supply the seeds for free. Planting, on the other hand, costs plants, labour and often protective measures.
106835.m: Natural regeneration saves plants and work.

106836.q: Why are naturally regenerated trees usually well adapted to where they grow?
a: Their parents already grew in the same place
They are modified in a laboratory
106836.e: The parent trees have coped with the climate and soil in the same place for decades. Their offspring carry these qualities.
106836.m: Trees from natural regeneration suit their site well.

106837.q: What are old trees called that are deliberately left standing during felling so that they supply the area with seeds?
106837.e: Seed trees scatter their seeds onto the open ground below. Once enough young trees have grown, they are often harvested later too.
106837.m: Seed trees supply an area with new seeds.

106838.q: What is a mast year in a forest?
a: A year with a particularly large number of seeds
A year with a particularly large amount of felling
A year with no rain at all
A year in which wild animals are fed
106838.e: In mast years, trees such as beech or oak bear an unusually large amount of fruit. Afterwards, a particularly large number of young trees sprout.
106838.m: In a mast year, trees produce a great many seeds.

106839.e: In afforestation, people plant young trees, for example after storm damage or on former pastures. Unlike natural regeneration, they choose the tree species.
106839.m: Afforestation means planting a new forest.

106840.q: Where are young trees raised for afforestation?
106840.e: In forest tree nurseries, the young plants grow from seed until they are strong enough to be planted out in the forest.
106840.m: Young plants for the forest are raised in a tree nursery.

106841.q: After which natural events did Switzerland begin large-scale reforestation of cleared mountain slopes in the 19th century?
106841.e: Bare mountain slopes could no longer hold back rainwater. After major floods, for example in 1868, people recognised the protective effect of forests.
106841.m: Forest on steep slopes protects against floods.

106842.q: What are the young trees called that are put into the ground during afforestation?
106842.e: Saplings are usually two to four years old when they are planted. They are put into the ground with a planting spade or a hoe.

106843.q: Why are barriers often built as well when reforesting steep avalanche slopes?
a: So that snow does not sweep the young trees away
So that tourists can climb there
So that wild animals find shelter
So that the ground gets warmer
106843.e: Young trees cannot yet stop moving snow. Barriers protect them until the forest itself works as a protection forest.

106844.q: What does the law usually require when forest may be removed for a building project?
106844.e: For every approved clearance, the same amount of forest must in principle be planted again, usually in the same area. This way the forest area is preserved.
106844.m: Cleared forest must usually be replaced.

106845.q: Why were almost only spruces often planted in afforestation on the Swiss Plateau in the past?
a: They grow fast and provide building timber
They are especially firm against storms
106845.e: Spruces promised a quick yield. Today we know that pure spruce stands in the lowlands are often not very stable.
106845.m: Pure spruce forests grow fast but are vulnerable.

106846.q: Which trees are preferably planted in afforestation today?
a: A mixture of species suited to the site
106846.e: Mixed forests of tree species that suit the site spread the risk. If one species fails, the others remain standing.

106847.q: According to the Forest Act, what usually has to be done if forest may be cleared as an exception?
a: Leave the land unused for ever
Build a wall around the area
Nothing more, the permit is enough
106847.e: For an approved clearance, a replacement must usually be provided in the same area, mostly as new forest. This way Switzerland's forest area is preserved.
106847.m: Anyone who clears forest usually has to plant new forest.

106848.q: Who is mainly responsible for enforcing the Forest Act in Switzerland?
106848.e: The federal government sets out the principles, and the cantons put them into practice with their own forestry services. For example, they approve fellings.
106848.m: The cantons put the Forest Act into practice.

106849.q: What does the Forest Act basically forbid?
106849.e: Forest clearance is turning forest permanently into other land, such as building land. An exception needs a permit for important reasons.
106849.m: In Switzerland, forest may basically not be cleared.

106850.q: According to the Forest Act, what may everyone do in a Swiss forest?
106850.e: The forest is meant to be open to the public. This also applies to privately owned forest.
106850.m: Anyone may enter the Swiss forest.

106851.q: What is basically not allowed in the forest and on forest roads?
106851.e: Motor vehicles may only use forests and forest roads for forestry work. There are special rules for exceptions.
106851.m: You may not drive into the forest by car.

106852.q: According to the Forest Act, what basically applies to forest that has grown by itself on an abandoned pasture?
a: It may be removed at any time
It automatically belongs to the federal government
106852.e: What matters is whether an area is actually covered with trees and fulfils forest functions. That is why newly grown forest is also basically protected.
106852.m: Forest that grew by itself is also forest in the eyes of the law.

106853.q: What does the Forest Act say about Switzerland's forest area?
a: It is to be doubled by 2050
It is set anew every year
106853.e: The forest is to be preserved in its area and its geographical distribution. This principle of forest conservation is at the heart of the law.
106853.m: The Swiss forest is not to get smaller.

106854.q: Which federal office is responsible for forests in Switzerland?
106854.e: The FOEN is the federal government's specialist office for forests. It prepares the groundwork and supports projects in the forest.
106854.m: The FOEN looks after the forest at federal level.

106855.q: Why was so much wood needed in the time of Hans Carl von Carlowitz?
a: For heating, building, and for mines and smelting furnaces
106855.e: Around 1700, wood was the most important fuel and building material. Mines and smelting works used huge amounts, so many forests were cleared completely.
106855.m: Around 1700, wood was the most important fuel and building material.

106856.q: What was the famous book by Hans Carl von Carlowitz about?
a: The forest and the use of wood
106856.e: In his “Sylvicultura oeconomica” of 1713, Carlowitz wrote about how to use the forest without destroying it.
106856.m: Carlowitz wrote a book about the forest.

106857.q: Which problem did Carlowitz warn about in his book?
106857.e: Mines, smelting works and towns used huge amounts of wood. Carlowitz feared that soon there would not be enough of it.
106857.m: Carlowitz warned of a shortage of wood.

106858.q: What fits Carlowitz's idea of sustainable forest use?
a: Planting young trees to replace felled ones
Felling the whole forest at once
Leaving felled areas empty for ever
106858.e: Carlowitz wanted the forest to last. So bare areas were to be replanted, and no more wood was to be cut than grows back.
106858.m: Sustainable means the forest is preserved even though it is used.

106859.q: Which word used by Carlowitz later developed into the German term for “sustainability” (Nachhaltigkeit)?
106859.e: Carlowitz called for a “continuirliche beständige und nachhaltende Nutzung” (continuous, lasting and sustaining use) of the forest. The word Nachhaltigkeit, sustainability, later came from this.
106859.m: Carlowitz spoke of a “nachhaltende”, sustaining use of the forest.

106860.q: Apart from using wood sparingly, what did Carlowitz recommend against the wood shortage?
106860.e: Carlowitz called for cleared areas to be stocked with trees again. In addition, better stoves were to use less wood.
106860.m: Carlowitz wanted to renew the forest by sowing and planting.

106861.q: When did Hans Carl von Carlowitz live?
106861.e: Carlowitz was born in 1645 and died in 1714. So he lived in the Baroque period.

106862.q: Which principle of forest use is mainly associated with Carlowitz today?
a: Cut only as much wood as grows back
Cut as much wood as possible at once
Fell only broadleaved trees, never conifers
106862.e: Carlowitz called for a balance between using wood and regrowth. This idea is at the heart of the principle of sustainability.
106862.m: Sustainable means not using more than grows back.

106863.q: What is the bark beetle called that causes the greatest forest damage in Switzerland?
106863.e: The European spruce bark beetle is only about half a centimetre long. But it can multiply in huge numbers.
106863.m: The European spruce bark beetle is Switzerland's most dangerous bark beetle.

106864.q: Which tree species does the European spruce bark beetle mainly attack?
106864.e: This beetle specialises in this conifer. Weakened trees at low altitudes are especially at risk.
106864.m: The European spruce bark beetle mainly attacks spruces.

106865.q: Where does the bark beetle make its breeding tunnels?
a: Between the bark and the wood
106865.e: The female lays her eggs in tunnels just under the bark. From there, the larvae eat side tunnels that form a typical pattern.
106865.m: Bark beetles breed just under the bark.

106866.q: Why does a tree badly infested by bark beetles die?
a: The tunnels cut off its flow of sap
The beetle eats all the needles
The tree becomes too heavy and topples over
106866.e: The feeding tunnels destroy the thin layer that carries water and nutrients. The crown is no longer supplied and dries out.
106866.m: Bark beetles cut off the tree's supply.

106867.q: How does a healthy spruce defend itself against bark beetles boring in?
106867.e: When a beetle bores in, sticky resin flows out. It can glue the beetle up or push it back out.

106868.q: Which weather helps bark beetles multiply in huge numbers?
106868.e: Warmth lets the beetles produce several generations a year more quickly. At the same time, the trees are weakened by lack of water.
106868.m: Heat and drought help bark beetles.

106869.q: What is the most important measure when a bark beetle infestation is discovered?
a: Quickly fell the infested trees and remove them
Water the tree heavily every day
106869.e: If infested spruces are quickly taken out of the forest or debarked, the young beetles cannot fly out. This slows down the spread.
106869.m: Infested trees must leave the forest quickly.

106870.q: From the outside, how can you often first spot a fresh bark beetle infestation?
a: By brown boring dust on the trunk
By red flowers in the crown
By white mould on the needles
By an unusually large number of cones
106870.e: Boring dust looks like fine ground coffee and collects in cracks in the bark and at the foot of the trunk. Later the crown changes colour.
106870.m: Brown boring dust gives bark beetles away.

106871.q: What are bark beetles lured into special traps with?
106871.e: Pheromones are scents the beetles use to attract one another. The traps are mainly used to monitor the number of beetles.
106871.m: Bark beetle traps work with lures.

106872.q: How much wood did Lothar blow down in Switzerland in 1999, compared with a normal annual harvest?
a: Almost three times an annual harvest
About a tenth of an annual harvest
About a hundredth of an annual harvest
106872.e: Lothar blew down about 13 million cubic metres of wood. That was almost three times as much as was harvested in Switzerland in a year at the time.
106872.m: Lothar blew down almost three annual harvests of wood.

106873.q: Which insects multiplied in huge numbers in the storm-felled wood in the years after Lothar?
106873.e: Fallen and weakened spruces offered ideal breeding places. As a result, many more trees died in the following years.
106873.m: After Lothar, bark beetles spread widely.

106874.q: In 1999, the storm Lothar blew down whole forests. What is such storm damage in a forest called?
106874.e: In windthrow, a storm blows trees over, roots and all, or snaps them. Lothar caused huge areas of windthrow in Switzerland.
106874.m: Trees blown over by a storm are called windthrow.

106875.q: Which areas of Switzerland did Lothar hit hardest?
a: The Swiss Plateau and the Prealps
The Engadine and the Val Poschiavo
106875.e: Lothar moved in from the west across the north side of the Alps. Especially in the cantons of Bern, Fribourg and Lucerne, whole forests lay on the ground.
106875.m: Lothar mainly hit the Swiss Plateau and the Prealps.

106876.q: Why was Lothar still dangerous even after the storm?
a: Clearing up led to fatal accidents
The roads stayed closed for years
106876.e: Fallen trees are often under great tension. When they are sawn up, trunks can spring up unexpectedly, which is why several people died during the clearing work.
106876.m: Clearing up storm-felled wood is very dangerous.

106877.q: Why did a particularly large number of spruces fall during the storm Lothar?
a: They lose their needles in winter
106877.e: Spruces form a flat root plate, especially on wet soils. So in strong wind they easily topple over, roots and all.
106877.m: Spruces have shallow roots and are easily blown over.

106878.q: What happened on many areas flattened by Lothar in the years that followed?
a: Young forest grew back without planting
They have stayed bare to this day
106878.e: Researchers observed that on many areas young trees quickly came up by themselves. The new forest was often more mixed than the old one.
106878.m: New forest often grows by itself on storm-damaged areas.

106879.q: What happened to the price of wood after the storm Lothar?
a: Wood could no longer be sold
106879.e: Suddenly there was far more wood in the forest than the sawmills could process. The large supply made prices collapse.
106879.m: After Lothar, the price of wood fell sharply.

106880.q: How was much of the storm-felled wood protected from fungi and insects after Lothar?
a: It was constantly sprinkled with water
It was buried in the ground
106880.e: In so-called wet storage sites, sprinklers keep the wood constantly damp. That way fungi and beetles cannot attack it.
106880.m: Wet storage keeps wood damp and so protects it.

106881.q: What is chopped-up wood called that is burnt automatically in large heating systems?
106881.e: For wood chips, branches, treetops and leftover wood are chopped into small pieces. Many municipalities heat school buildings with them.
106881.m: Wood chips are chopped-up wood for heating.

106882.q: Why is heating with wood from sustainable forestry considered almost carbon-neutral?
a: The tree absorbed the CO2 while growing
Wood burns with no exhaust gases at all
106882.e: When it burns, about as much CO2 is released as the tree took in from the air before. If the same amount of forest grows back, the balance stays almost even.
106882.m: When burnt, wood releases the CO2 it absorbed while growing.

106883.q: Why should firewood be well dried before burning?
a: It gives more heat and less smoke
Wet wood burns far too hot
106883.e: In wet wood, the water must evaporate first, and that takes energy. Wet wood also smokes and produces more soot.

106884.q: What is the unit for one cubic metre of stacked firewood with gaps?
106884.e: A stere is a cube with sides of one metre, filled with stacked logs. Because there is air in between, it contains less wood than a solid cubic metre.
106884.m: A stere is one cubic metre of stacked wood.

106885.q: Which pollutant is mainly produced by badly operated wood-burning systems?
106885.e: Incomplete burning produces tiny particles of soot and dust. They can get deep into the lungs.
106885.m: Badly burning wood fires produce a lot of fine dust.

106886.q: What is a network of pipes called that delivers hot water from a central wood-fired heating plant to many houses?
106886.e: The heat is produced in a large heating plant and distributed through insulated pipes. That way the individual houses do not need their own stove.
106886.m: A district heating network distributes heat to many houses.

106887.q: Which stove stores the heat of a wood fire in heavy stones and gives it off for hours?
106887.e: The fire heats up the thick walls of stone and ceramic. They give off heat long after the fire has gone out.
106887.m: A tiled stove stores heat for a long time.

106888.q: What causes most forest fires in Switzerland?
106888.e: Discarded cigarettes, unattended fires or sparks from machines cause most fires.
106888.m: Most forest fires are caused by people.

106889.q: Which Swiss canton has the most forest fires?
106889.e: On the south side of the Alps the climate is mild, and there are long dry spells again and again. Many slopes are also steep and hard to reach.
106889.m: Forest fires are most frequent in Ticino.

106890.q: In which season are forest fires particularly common in Ticino?
106890.e: At that time dry leaves lie on the ground, the plants are not yet green, and a dry north wind often blows.
106890.m: In Ticino, late winter is forest fire season.

106891.q: What usually grows back first on an area burnt by a forest fire?
a: Nothing at all for a hundred years
106891.e: On the burnt area above Leuk in the Valais, which burnt in 2003, herbs, grasses and shrubs grew first. It takes decades before a forest stands there again.
106891.m: After a forest fire, herbs and shrubs come back first.

106892.q: How do helicopters fight forest fires on steep ground?
a: With a water container on a rope
106892.e: The helicopters fill the container in a lake or river and release the water right over the fire.
106892.m: Firefighting helicopters fetch water from lakes and rivers.

106893.q: What do the authorities often order when the risk of forest fires is high?
a: A ban on fires in the forest
A ban on swimming in lakes
106893.e: In dry weather, a single spark can start a fire. Then fire is banned in and near the forest, often even in permanent fireplaces.
106893.m: In dry weather, there is often a ban on fires in the forest.

106894.q: Which natural event can start a forest fire without any human involvement?
106894.e: If lightning strikes a tree, dry wood can catch fire. Such fires start mainly during summer thunderstorms.

106895.q: Why are forest fires on steep mountain slopes particularly problematic?
a: Afterwards protection from natural hazards is missing
Afterwards the ground freezes for ever
Afterwards no animal can live there any more
106895.e: Burnt slopes can no longer slow down rockfall, avalanches and debris flows. It takes decades for a new protection forest to grow back.
106895.m: After a fire, the protection forest is often missing.

106896.q: What is meant by browsing damage?
a: Wild animals eat the buds and shoots of young trees
Wild animals rub their antlers on trunks
Woodpeckers peck holes in the bark
106896.e: In browsing, animals such as roe deer or red deer nibble off the tips of young trees. Especially in winter, they find little other food.
106896.m: Browsing is wild animals eating young shoots.

106897.q: Which wild animal causes the most browsing damage on the Swiss Plateau?
106897.e: Roe deer are very common on the Swiss Plateau. They like to feed on buds and young shoots.
106897.m: On the Swiss Plateau, browsing is mainly caused by roe deer.

106898.q: Which conifer species suffers particularly badly from browsing in Switzerland?
106898.e: Wild animals prefer to eat young silver firs. In some forests, hardly any young firs grow up any more.
106898.m: Wild animals particularly like to browse silver firs.

106899.q: Why is it particularly harmful when wild animals eat the leading shoot of a young tree?
a: The young tree hardly grows any taller
The young tree stops forming flowers
The young tree loses its roots
The young tree turns brown at once
106899.e: The leading shoot is the top shoot that makes the tree grow upwards. If it is eaten again and again, the young tree stays small and bushy.
106899.m: Without a leading shoot, a young tree hardly grows upwards.

106900.q: How can individual young trees be protected from browsing?
a: With wire cages or tree shelters
With salt licks put up nearby
106900.e: The shelters stop roe deer and red deer from reaching the shoots. Once the tree is big enough, they are removed again.
106900.m: Wire cages protect young trees from browsing.

106901.q: What effect does heavy browsing have on the make-up of a forest?
a: Fewer different tree species grow up
The forest becomes richer in species
106901.e: Wild animals prefer to eat certain tree species. The less popular species are left, and the forest becomes more uniform.
106901.m: Heavy browsing makes the forest poorer in species.

106902.q: Which measure do the cantons use to regulate wild animal numbers and limit browsing?
106902.e: Hunting plans take into account the state of the young forest. The aim is a balance between forest and wildlife.
106902.m: Hunting helps keep forest and wildlife in balance.

106903.q: Which large wild animal with antlers causes a lot of browsing, especially in mountain forests?
106903.e: Red deer often live in herds and in winter eat buds, shoots and even bark. In the Grisons, their numbers are large.
106903.m: Red deer cause a lot of browsing in mountain forests.

106904.q: What is the Swiss National Forest Inventory?
a: A regular survey of the state of the forest
A list of all foresters in Switzerland
A forest festival in every canton
106904.e: For the National Forest Inventory, trees are measured and counted all over the country. That way we know how the Swiss forest is doing.
106904.m: The National Forest Inventory shows the state of the Swiss forest.

106905.q: Why is the National Forest Inventory repeated every few years?
a: To detect changes in the forest
Because the trees move every year
Because the old figures get lost
106905.e: The first inventory was made in the 1980s. Repeating it shows whether the forest is growing, how much wood grows back and how biodiversity is doing.
106905.m: Repeated measurements show how the forest is changing.

106906.q: How does the growing stock per hectare in the Swiss forest compare with the rest of Europe?
106906.e: Many Swiss forests are dense and old because less wood is used than grows back. That is why there is a particularly large amount of wood per hectare.
106906.m: There is a great deal of wood per hectare in the Swiss forest.

106907.q: Which feature relating to biodiversity does the National Forest Inventory also record?
106907.e: Dead trees are a habitat for beetles, fungi, mosses and woodpeckers. That is why their amount is an important sign of how natural a forest is.

106908.q: What does the growing stock of a forest indicate?
a: The volume of all living trunks
The amount of firewood in storage
The weight of all the leaves
106908.e: The growing stock is given in cubic metres. It shows how much wood is standing in the forest right now.
106908.m: The growing stock is the wood standing in the forest.

106909.q: How does the National Forest Inventory obtain its data?
106909.e: Sample plots on a regular grid are visited all over the country and the trees are measured. Aerial photos and surveys of the forestry services are added to this.
106909.m: The National Forest Inventory measures trees on many sample plots.

106910.q: How has Switzerland's forest area developed in recent decades?
a: It has increased, especially in the Alps
It has stayed exactly the same
It has increased only in towns
106910.e: Shrubs and trees grow by themselves on abandoned alpine pastures and mountain meadows. That way new forest gradually forms there.
106910.m: The Swiss forest is growing, especially in the Alps.

106911.q: Who owns most of the Swiss forest?
106911.e: About two thirds of the forest belongs to municipalities, civic communities, corporations or cantons. The rest is mostly privately owned in small plots.
106911.m: Most of the Swiss forest belongs to public bodies.

106912.q: At what height is the diameter of a tree trunk measured in forest inventories?
a: In the middle of the trunk
106912.e: This is called the diameter at breast height. Because it is always measured at the same height, the values can be compared well.
106912.m: The trunk diameter is measured at breast height.

107013.q: Which blood vessels are the finest in the human body?
107013.e: Capillaries, also called hair vessels, are the smallest blood vessels. They form a fine network that runs through almost all tissues.
107013.m: The capillaries are the finest blood vessels in the body.

107014.q: How thick is the wall of a capillary?
107014.e: The wall of a capillary is made of just one thin layer of endothelial cells. That is why substances can pass through it easily.
107014.m: Capillaries have a wafer-thin wall of just one layer of cells.

107015.q: What is the main job of the capillaries?
a: Exchanging substances between blood and tissue
107015.e: In the capillaries, oxygen and nutrients pass from the blood into the tissue. In return, the blood takes up carbon dioxide and waste.
107015.m: In the capillaries, blood and tissue exchange substances.

107016.q: Roughly what is the diameter of a typical capillary?
107016.e: Capillaries are only about 5 to 10 micrometres wide, which is much thinner than a hair. A micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre.
107016.m: A capillary is much thinner than a human hair.

107017.q: How do red blood cells move through the narrowest capillaries?
a: Not at all, they stay still
107017.e: The narrowest capillaries are hardly wider than a red blood cell. The blood cells change shape and squeeze through one at a time.
107017.m: In narrow capillaries, red blood cells line up one by one.

107018.q: Between which blood vessels do the capillaries lie?
a: Between the windpipe and the lungs
Between the stomach and the intestines
107018.e: The blood flows from the arteries through the fine capillaries into the veins and from there back to the heart.
107018.m: The capillaries connect arteries and veins.

107019.q: Which gas do the capillaries in a working muscle mainly give off?
107019.e: The blood brings oxygen to the muscle cells, which need it to make energy. In return the blood takes up carbon dioxide.
107019.m: In muscles, the capillaries give oxygen to the cells.

107020.q: Where do capillaries in the lungs take up oxygen?
107020.e: The air sacs (alveoli) are surrounded by dense networks of capillaries. There, oxygen passes from the air you breathe into the blood.
107020.m: A network of capillaries surrounds the air sacs in the lungs.

107021.q: How fast does blood flow in the capillaries compared with the large arteries?
107021.e: All the capillaries together have a huge total cross-section, so the blood flows very slowly there. This leaves enough time for substances to be exchanged.
107021.m: Blood flows slowly in the capillaries so that the exchange can happen.

107022.q: What is the large artery in the groin that supplies the leg with blood called?
107022.e: The femoral artery, in Latin arteria femoralis, runs from the groin down the thigh. It is the main artery of the leg.
107022.m: The leg is mainly supplied by the femoral artery.

107023.q: Which artery is squeezed by the cuff when blood pressure is measured?
a: The brachial artery in the upper arm
107023.e: The cuff goes round the upper arm and squeezes the artery there. Its Latin name is arteria brachialis.
107023.m: When measuring blood pressure, the upper arm artery is briefly squeezed.

107024.q: Which artery runs along the little-finger side of the forearm?
107024.e: The forearm has two main arteries along its two bones. The ulna is on the little-finger side, and the ulnar artery runs next to it.
107024.m: The ulnar artery runs next to the ulna on the little-finger side.

107025.q: On which side of the wrist do you usually feel for the pulse?
a: On the back of the hand
In the middle of the palm
107025.e: On the thumb side of the wrist, the radial artery runs just under the skin. There the pulse can easily be felt with two fingers.
107025.m: You feel the pulse at the wrist on the thumb side.

107026.q: How does blood pressure change the further the blood gets from the heart?
a: It stays exactly the same everywhere
107026.e: The heart creates the pressure, and some of it is constantly lost through friction in the ever finer vessels. In the veins, the pressure is finally very low.
107026.m: The further from the heart, the lower the blood pressure.

107027.e: The pulmonary artery takes oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. It is still an artery, because it carries blood away from the heart.
107027.m: The pulmonary artery is an artery with oxygen-poor blood.

107028.q: Why do arteries have thicker walls than veins?
a: The blood pressure in them is higher
They lie right under the skin
107028.e: The heart pumps the blood into the arteries at high pressure. Their thick, muscular walls withstand this pressure.
107028.m: Arteries have thick walls because of the high pressure.

107029.q: What are the smallest branches of the arteries called?
107029.e: Arterioles are tiny arteries that lead the blood into the hair vessels. By getting narrower or wider, they control the blood supply.
107029.m: The smallest arteries are called arterioles.

107030.q: Which painless examination is used to check the carotid artery for narrowing?
107030.e: With an ultrasound device, the carotid artery can be viewed from outside and the blood flow measured. This shows narrowing without any operation.
107030.m: Narrowing of the carotid artery is found with ultrasound.

107031.q: How many common carotid arteries does a person have?
107031.e: There is a left and a right common carotid artery. Each supplies its own side of the head and neck.
107031.m: People have one carotid artery on the left and one on the right.

107032.q: Where can you feel the pulse well on the neck?
a: At the side of the neck, on the carotid artery
At the back of the neck, on the spine
At the front, on the voice box
Under the chin, on the bone
107032.e: The carotid artery lies at the side of the neck just under the skin. If you put two fingers there, you feel the blood throbbing with every heartbeat.
107032.m: At the side of the neck you can feel the pulse of the carotid artery.

107033.q: Into which two branches does the common carotid artery split?
107033.e: At about the level of the voice box, the common carotid artery forks. This forms the internal and the external carotid artery.
107033.m: The common carotid artery forks into an inner and an outer branch.

107034.q: Which organ does the internal carotid artery mainly supply?
107034.e: The internal carotid artery passes through the base of the skull into the inside of the head. There it supplies large parts of the brain and the eye with blood.
107034.m: The internal carotid artery brings blood to the brain.

107035.q: What does the external carotid artery supply?
107035.e: The external carotid artery stays outside the skull. Its branches supply the face, tongue, scalp and neck, among other parts.
107035.m: The external carotid artery supplies the face and neck.

107036.q: From which organ does the blood that flows through the carotid artery come?
107036.e: The heart pumps the blood into the aorta. The carotid arteries branch off from it and take the blood to the head.
107036.m: The carotid artery takes blood from the heart to the head.

107037.q: What do sensory cells at the fork of the carotid artery measure?
107037.e: The carotid sinus with its pressure sensors sits at the fork. They report the blood pressure to the brain so that it can control it.
107037.m: Sensors on the carotid artery measure blood pressure.

107038.q: To which organ does the portal vein take the blood?
107038.e: The portal vein collects blood from the stomach and intestines and takes it to the liver first. Only after that does it flow on to the heart.
107038.m: The portal vein leads to the liver.

107039.q: From which organs does the portal vein collect blood?
a: From the stomach, intestines and spleen
107039.e: Veins from the stomach, intestines, spleen and pancreas flow into the portal vein. In this way their blood reaches the liver first.
107039.m: The portal vein collects the blood of the digestive organs.

107040.q: After a meal, what does the blood in the portal vein contain in especially large amounts?
107040.e: The intestines absorb nutrients such as sugar and amino acids into the blood. Through the portal vein they reach the liver first, which processes them.
107040.m: After eating, the portal vein carries lots of nutrients.

107041.q: What is special about the portal vein?
a: It is a vein that leads into an organ instead of to the heart
It is an artery with no wall at all
It pumps the blood itself like a heart
It carries air instead of blood
107041.e: Normal veins take the blood back to the heart. The portal vein, by contrast, connects the network of capillaries in the intestines with a second network of capillaries in the liver.
107041.m: The portal vein is a vein between two networks of capillaries.

107042.q: What kind of blood flows in the portal vein?
a: Oxygen-poor blood from the digestive organs
107042.e: The portal vein is a vein. It carries blood from the stomach, intestines and spleen that has already given up oxygen but contains lots of nutrients.
107042.m: The portal vein carries blood from the digestive organs.

107043.q: Where does the portal vein get its name from?
a: It leads into the liver as if through a gate
It lies just behind the mouth
A researcher called Portal discovered it
It is as wide as a door
107043.e: The Latin word porta means gate. The portal vein enters the liver at a kind of entrance gate.
107043.m: The portal vein is the gate to the liver.

107044.q: What does the liver do with many substances from the portal vein blood?
a: It processes them and removes poisons
107044.e: The liver stores nutrients, converts them and makes poisonous substances harmless. That is why it makes sense for the blood from the intestines to flow through the liver first.
107044.m: The liver cleans and processes the blood from the portal vein.

107045.q: Which liver disease often leads to high pressure in the portal vein?
107045.e: In cirrhosis of the liver, the liver tissue becomes scarred and hard. The blood then backs up in the portal vein in front of the liver.
107045.m: A scarred liver can cause a blockage in the portal vein.

107046.q: Why should you measure on several days if high blood pressure is suspected?
a: Because blood pressure goes up and down during the day
Because you may only measure on Sundays
Because one measurement is always wrong
107046.e: Blood pressure changes with movement, stress, time of day and sleep. Only several measurements give a reliable picture.
107046.m: A single blood pressure reading says little; only many readings show the picture.

107047.q: What does the upper blood pressure reading show?
a: The pressure when the heart contracts
The pressure in the lungs when breathing in
The number of heartbeats per minute
The amount of blood in the body
107047.e: The upper reading is called the systolic blood pressure. It is produced when the ventricles contract and push blood into the arteries.
107047.m: The upper blood pressure reading is the pressure during a heartbeat.

107048.q: What does the lower blood pressure reading show?
a: The pressure when the heart relaxes
The pressure when the heart contracts
The number of heartbeats per minute
The amount of blood in the body
107048.e: Between two beats, the heart relaxes and fills with blood. The pressure in the arteries then drops to the lower reading.
107048.m: The lower blood pressure reading is the pressure while the heart rests.

107049.q: What is used to measure blood pressure on the upper arm?
107049.e: The cuff is put round the upper arm and pumped up. As it is slowly let down, the device measures the blood pressure.
107049.m: Blood pressure is measured with an arm cuff.

107050.q: What is the measurement called in which a portable device measures blood pressure regularly for a whole day?
107050.e: For 24-hour blood pressure monitoring, you wear a cuff with a small device for 24 hours. It also measures automatically during the night.
107050.m: 24-hour blood pressure monitoring records blood pressure over a whole day.

107051.q: Which instrument does the doctor use to hear the sounds in the arm when measuring blood pressure?
107051.e: The stethoscope is placed in the crook of the arm under the cuff. In this way you can hear the blood knocking and read off the blood pressure.
107051.m: A stethoscope lets you hear sounds inside the body.

107052.q: What is meant by “white coat hypertension”?
a: Blood pressure is only raised at the doctor’s because of nerves
Blood pressure rises when you wear white clothes
Blood pressure is always raised in winter
Blood pressure is only measured by doctors
107052.e: Some people are nervous at the doctor’s surgery, and their blood pressure rises there. At home their readings are then normal.
107052.m: Nerves at the doctor’s can raise the measured blood pressure.

107053.q: At what height should the cuff be when measuring blood pressure?
a: At the level of the feet
107053.e: If the cuff is higher or lower than the heart, the reading is wrong. That is why the arm should be placed so that the cuff is at heart level.
107053.m: When measuring blood pressure, the cuff belongs at heart level.

107055.q: Which mineral, found in large amounts in vegetables and fruit, can help to lower blood pressure?
107055.e: Potassium helps the body get rid of sodium through the kidneys and relaxes the blood vessels. Vegetables, fruit and pulses contain lots of it.
107055.m: A diet rich in potassium with plenty of vegetables is good for blood pressure.

107056.q: Which feature of the body clearly increases the risk of high blood pressure?
107056.e: When someone is very overweight, the heart has to work harder and the blood vessels are under more strain. Even losing some weight can lower blood pressure.
107056.m: Being very overweight strains the heart and blood pressure.

107057.q: Why do many people not notice their high blood pressure for a long time?
a: It often causes no symptoms for a long time
It turns the skin blue straight away
107057.e: High blood pressure usually does not hurt and causes no symptoms for a long time. That is why it is often only discovered when it is measured.
107057.m: You often cannot feel high blood pressure, so you should have it measured.

107058.q: Which seasoning can raise blood pressure if you eat a lot of it?
107058.e: Lots of table salt holds water in the body and can make blood pressure rise in many people. Ready meals often contain lots of hidden salt.
107058.m: Too much salt can push blood pressure up.

107059.q: Which brain condition becomes more likely after years of high blood pressure?
107059.e: Over time, high pressure damages the walls of the blood vessels. This increases the risk that a vessel in the brain becomes blocked or bursts.
107059.m: Untreated high blood pressure increases the risk of a stroke.

107060.q: What helps most to prevent high blood pressure?
107060.e: Regular exercise strengthens the heart and blood vessels and helps keep a healthy weight. Both lower the risk of high blood pressure.
107060.m: Regular exercise protects your blood vessels.

107061.q: What is the opposite of high blood pressure, meaning blood pressure that is too low, called?
107061.e: The prefix “hypo” means under or too little. That is why blood pressure that is low all the time is called hypotension.
107061.m: Blood pressure that is too low is called hypotension.

107062.q: Which organs that filter the blood can high blood pressure damage?
107062.e: The kidneys contain many fine vessels that filter the blood. Constant high pressure can damage these vessels and make the kidneys work less well.
107062.m: High blood pressure can damage the kidneys.

107063.q: Which drink raises blood pressure if you regularly drink a lot of it?
107063.e: Regularly drinking a lot of alcohol is one of the known causes of high blood pressure. Drinking less alcohol can lower blood pressure again.
107063.m: Lots of alcohol can raise blood pressure for good.

107064.q: What is the technical term for a short faint?
107064.e: A syncope is a short loss of consciousness from which you quickly recover. The term comes from Greek.
107064.m: A short faint is called a syncope.

a: The brain briefly gets too little blood
107065.e: In a faint, the brain briefly gets too little blood. As a result it lacks oxygen and you lose consciousness for a short time.
107065.m: In a faint, the brain briefly gets too little blood.

107066.q: How do you help a person who has briefly fainted and is breathing normally?
a: Lay them flat and raise their legs
Stand them up at once and make them walk
Give them cold water to drink
107066.e: If the legs are raised, more blood flows to the heart and brain. The person then usually comes round quickly.
107066.m: When someone faints, raise their legs.

107067.q: How long does an ordinary faint usually last?
a: Only seconds to a few minutes
107067.e: With a syncope, you quickly come round by yourself, usually after seconds. If the unconsciousness lasts longer, medical help is needed.
107067.m: An ordinary faint is over after a short time.

107068.q: Which situation can trigger a faint especially easily?
a: Standing for a long time in great heat
107068.e: When you stand for a long time in the heat, the blood vessels widen and blood collects in the legs. The brain then lacks blood.
107068.m: Standing for a long time in the heat can lead to fainting.

107069.q: Which warning sign often comes before a faint?
a: Everything goes black before your eyes
107069.e: Before a faint, dizziness, blackouts in your vision and nausea often occur. If you notice this, it is best to sit or lie down straight away.
107069.m: If everything goes black before your eyes, sit down straight away.

107070.q: A person stays unconscious but is breathing normally. How do you position them?
a: On their front with the face down
107070.e: In the recovery position, the airways stay clear and vomit can drain away. Then you call for help and keep checking the breathing.
107070.m: Unconscious people who breathe normally go into the recovery position.

107071.q: Why do some people briefly faint at the sight of blood?
a: A nerve reaction suddenly lowers pulse and blood pressure
The blood evaporates and makes you tired
The eyes are dazzled by the red
The stomach pulls all the blood towards it
107071.e: In this so-called vasovagal syncope, the nervous system overreacts. Heartbeat and blood pressure drop briefly, and the brain gets too little blood.
107071.m: A fright or the sight of blood can trigger a faint through the nerves.

107072.q: What happens in a circulatory collapse?
107072.e: In a circulatory collapse, blood pressure suddenly drops. The brain gets less blood, you feel weak and can collapse.
107072.m: A circulatory collapse is a sudden drop in blood pressure.

107073.q: Which movement makes some people dizzy because their blood pressure drops?
a: Getting up too quickly from lying down
Breathing out deeply while lying down
107073.e: When you get up quickly, blood flows into the legs before the circulation has adjusted. For a moment, the brain gets too little blood.
107073.m: If you get up quickly, your blood pressure can drop for a moment.

107074.q: When you stand still for a long time, where does a lot of blood pool?
107074.e: Because of gravity, blood collects in the veins of the legs. Without muscle movement, it only flows back to the heart slowly.
107074.m: When you stand for a long time, blood collects in the legs.

107075.q: What helps prevent a circulatory collapse on hot days?
a: Standing in the sun for a long time
107075.e: In the heat, the body loses a lot of fluid through sweating. If the blood is short of fluid, blood pressure drops more easily.
107075.m: Drinking enough in the heat protects your circulation.

107076.q: What helps against a circulatory collapse when standing for a long time?
a: Moving your toes and calves again and again
Holding your breath as long as possible
Holding your arms high above your head
107076.e: Working calf muscles squeeze the veins and push the blood towards the heart. This muscle pump keeps the circulation going.
107076.m: Moving calf muscles pump the blood back from the legs.

107077.q: What is a circulatory collapse caused by great heat called?
107077.e: In great heat, the blood vessels in the skin widen to give off warmth. This can make blood pressure drop so much that a heat collapse happens.
107077.m: Great heat can cause a heat collapse.

107078.q: What does the skin often look like during a circulatory collapse?
107078.e: In a collapse, the blood vessels in the skin narrow and a cold sweat breaks out. That is why the person looks pale.
107078.m: In a circulatory collapse, the skin is often pale and damp.

107079.q: What should you be careful about when getting up after a circulatory collapse?
a: Sit up slowly and only then stand up
Jump up at once and run
107079.e: The circulation needs time to recover. If you get up too quickly, you risk collapsing again.
107079.m: After a collapse, get up again only slowly.

a: Hardening and narrowing of the arteries
107080.e: In arteriosclerosis, substances build up in the artery wall. The artery becomes hard, narrow and less elastic.
107080.m: Arteriosclerosis makes the arteries hard and narrow.

107081.q: What is arteriosclerosis often called in everyday language?
107081.e: Because the deposits also contain lime (calcium), people often call it hardening of the arteries. The medical term is arteriosclerosis.
107081.m: In everyday language, arteriosclerosis is called hardening of the arteries.

107082.q: What are the deposits in the artery walls called?
